This section contains the complete activity instructions. The starter loads the data and supplies spaces to record your work. Open activity08.ipynb from the folder prepared in Set Up Your Chapter Files, using the same project environment. The worked examples above are preparation, not additional submission requirements.
You will use the same Palmer penguins dataset the chapter uses, loaded the same way, so the activity needs no data file of its own.

A. One Numeric Variable, and What the Bins Decide

Replace Your Name in the opening Raw cell’s author field. Run the setup cell; it must report the shape (344, 7).
Draw flipper_length_mm as a histogram with 5 bins, then 15, then 40, and describe the shape each one shows in a sentence. Say which bin count you would report, and why.
Report how many penguins the histogram left out because the column is missing, and show the code that told you. Nothing on the plot itself says so.
Draw the same column as a density curve and as a box plot. Name one thing each of the three views shows that the other two hide.



B. One Categorical Variable, in Two Libraries

Count the penguins on each island and draw the counts as a bar chart, with the bars in decreasing order of count.
Draw that same bar chart twice: once with pandas and once with seaborn.
In two or three sentences, compare the two versions: which ordered the bars with less work, which labelled the axes for you, and which you would use for a quick look versus for a report.



C. Two Numeric Variables, and a Line Only Where It Belongs

Display the correlation matrix of the four numeric columns and draw it as a heatmap with the colour scale pinned to the full −1 to +1 range. Read off the correlation between bill_depth_mm and body_mass_g and interpret its sign in a sentence.
Draw the scatter plot of those two columns, then redraw it with hue="species".
Fit a regression line to the pooled data with sns.regplot, then say what happens to the relationship inside each species. Explain what the pooled line claims and why that claim is wrong for these penguins.
Finish with one sentence on what this means for reading a correlation computed over a mixed population.



D. Groups, Hidden Aggregation, and a Finished Plot

Compare body_mass_g across the three species with a box plot, and then with sns.barplot.
The bar chart shows one height per species although you never averaged anything. Say what seaborn computed for you, what the thin vertical line on each bar represents, and which of the two plots you would put in a report.
Redraw your chosen plot as a finished figure: both axes labelled with units, a title that states a finding rather than the mechanics, and a deliberate figure size. Save it as a 300-dpi PNG and confirm the saved file is not blank.
Explain in one sentence why a bar chart of these means has to start at zero.



Render and Submit
Restart the kernel, run all cells in order, resolve unexpected errors, and save. Include your plots, outputs, and explanations for A–D, and a short Markdown completion note. From stat303-data-visualization-1 in the terminal, run:
quarto render activity08.ipynb --to html
Follow the Quarto refresher: inspect the HTML and a copy opened outside the project folder, and confirm that every plot appears and your name is on the report. Upload only activity08.html to the Data Visualization I Canvas quiz; keep your notebook locally.

Use the correlation heatmap to pick the pair of numeric columns with the weakest correlation, and draw that pair with sns.regplot. Would you report this line to someone? title: 8  Data Visualization I: Choosing and Drawing a Single Plot
text:
8.16 Before You Move On
The habit to carry forward is choosing before drawing: count the variables, check their types, and let the question pick the plot. Reach for the library that fits the job — pandas for a glance at a DataFrame you already have, seaborn for anything involving groups or distributions, and plt.* for the labels, size, and saving, whichever library drew the picture.
The plotting libraries are also quietly summarizing your data — binning it, counting it, averaging it — before they draw a single pixel. Understanding what a plot computed is as important as knowing which plot to pick.
For any plot you make or read, you should be able to answer five questions without redrawing it:

What question is this plot answering, and do the variable types fit that question?
What did the library compute before it drew — bins, counts, means, quartiles, a fitted line?
How many observations are missing from the picture because a value was missing, and where did that number come from?
Does the pattern in the pooled data still hold inside each group?
Would a reader who saw only this picture reach the conclusion the data supports — axes labelled with units, a title that states the finding, and bars starting at zero?

Continue to Data Visualization II, where several plots are combined into one figure so that groups and variables can be compared side by side.
References: seaborn function overview, distributions tutorial, histplot, regplot, heatmap, pandas plotting, matplotlib pyplot tutorial, and the penguin measurements of Gorman, Williams, and Fraser (2014).

title: 9  Data Visualization II: Interfaces, Subplots, and Multi-Panel Figures
text:
9.1 Set Up Your Chapter Files
Every plot in Data Visualization I was a single picture drawn with a single command. We wrote plt.hist(...) or sns.boxplot(...), added labels, and a figure appeared. We never had to ask where it appeared, because there was only one place it could go.
That question — where does this plot go? — is what this chapter is about. Once you want two plots side by side, or a grid of six, you need to name the thing you are drawing into. Doing that requires learning:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:
Complete the practice activity after the worked examples.
Download the Data Visualization II practice kit. Extract stat303-data-visualization-2 inside the chapters folder of your stat303-1 course folder, open stat303-1 in VS Code, and select the course environment. The terminal opens in stat303-1, so move it into the kit with cd chapters and then cd stat303-data-visualization-2 before you render the activity.
Run data_viz_2_examples.ipynb for the lesson and complete activity09.ipynb for your own activity report, with stat303-data-visualization-2 as the notebook working folder.
This kit has no data/ folder, and nothing belongs in one. As in the previous chapter, every figure uses the Palmer penguins dataset that comes with seaborn, which sns.load_dataset("penguins") hands you in one line. The first call downloads the file and caches it on your computer, so you need a network connection once; after that it loads from the cache. If you would rather read it from a file of your own, the note under The data in the previous chapter shows the one-line change.
The three libraries and the aliases pd, plt, and sns are the same as in Data Visualization I.
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins")
df.head()








species
island

title: 9  Data Visualization II: Interfaces, Subplots, and Multi-Panel Figures
text:
9.2 Anatomy of a figure
Matplotlib’s vocabulary is the first thing that trips people up, because two of its central words look almost identical. Learn these four terms and most documentation suddenly becomes readable.
Figure — the whole canvas. It is the sheet of paper. A figure has a size (figsize=(width, height) in inches), and it is the thing you save to a file. A figure can hold one panel or twenty.
Axes — one panel: a single plot with its own x-axis, y-axis, title, and data. This is the confusing one. Despite sounding plural, one Axes object is one rectangular plot. A figure with six panels contains six Axes. Whenever you read “axes” in matplotlib documentation or in a variable name like ax, read it as “panel” and you will rarely be confused.
Axis — one of the actual number lines, the x-axis or the y-axis, belonging to an Axes. You will interact with these much less often than with Axes.
Artist — everything drawable: each line, bar, dot, piece of text, tick, and legend. Everything you see on a figure is an Artist, including the Axes themselves.
The containment goes one way:
Figure  (the canvas, what you save)
└── Axes  (a panel — one plot; there can be many)
    ├── Axis  (the x number line)
    ├── Axis  (the y number line)
    └── Artists  (the bars, dots, lines, text, legend)






TipAxes vs. Axis



Axes = one panel. Axis = one number line. The plural of Axes is also “axes”, which is why people say “a figure with three axes” meaning three panels. If a sentence seems to be using the word strangely, substitute “panel” and see if it makes sense.


In the last chapter, every plot created one Figure containing exactly one Axes — we just never referred to either of them by name.

title: 9  Data Visualization II: Interfaces, Subplots, and Multi-Panel Figures
text:
9.3 The two interfaces
Matplotlib gives you two different ways to draw the same plot. This is the main reason matplotlib code found online looks inconsistent: you are seeing two styles mixed together, sometimes in the same code block. Once you can tell them apart, the confusion mostly disappears.

9.3.1 Interface 1: pyplot, the implicit interface
This is what the last chapter used. You call functions on plt directly, and matplotlib keeps track of a “current figure” and a “current Axes” behind the scenes. Every plt. command you issue applies to whatever is current.

plt.hist(df["body_mass_g"], bins=15)
plt.xlabel("Body mass (g)")
plt.ylabel("Number of penguins")
plt.title("Made with the pyplot interface")
plt.show()








There is no variable anywhere in that code holding the figure or the panel. plt.hist noticed that no figure existed, created one with a single Axes, made it current, and drew into it. The next three commands each modified “the current Axes” — that same one.
This style is called the implicit interface, because the panel each command draws into is implied rather than named.
It is excellent for one quick plot, and that is exactly what we used it for.


9.3.2 Interface 2: the object-oriented, explicit interface
Here you ask for the figure and panel up front, keep them in variables, and call methods on those variables:

fig, ax = plt.subplots()

ax.hist(df["body_mass_g"], bins=15)
ax.set_xlabel("Body mass (g)")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of penguins")
ax.set_title("Made with the object-oriented interface")
plt.show()








The same picture, with one important difference: nothing is implied. plt.subplots() creates a Figure and an Axes and hands both back, so fig is the canvas and ax is the panel. Every subsequent command says explicitly which panel it is drawing into.
Read that first line carefully, because it appears in nearly every matplotlib program you will ever write:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
plt.subplots() returns two things, and the two names on the left unpack them: fig is the Figure, ax is the Axes. You can name them anything, but fig and ax are the universal convention.
This is called the object-oriented (OO) or explicit interface.


9.3.3 The translation table
The two interfaces do the same things under slightly different names. The pattern is that most plt.something(...) functions become ax.set_something(...) methods:







pyplot (implicit)
object-oriented (explicit)




plt.plot(...), plt.hist(...), plt.scatter(...)
ax.plot(...), ax.hist(...), ax.scatter(...)


plt.xlabel("x")
ax.set_xlabel("x")


plt.ylabel("y")
ax.set_ylabel("y")


plt.title("t")
ax.set_title("t")


plt.xlim(0, 10)
ax.set_xlim(0, 10)


plt.xticks(rotation=45)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45)


plt.legend()
ax.legend()


plt.savefig("f.png")
fig.savefig("f.png")


(no equivalent)
fig.suptitle("figure-wide title")



Note the two sides of the split: plotting commands keep their names (plt.hist → ax.hist) while labelling commands gain a set_ prefix (plt.xlabel → ax.set_xlabel). And notice which object each belongs to: anything about one panel is a method of ax, while anything about the whole canvas — saving, a figure-wide title — is a method of fig.






NoteSetting several properties at once



Because the set_ methods all belong to the Axes, there is a shortcut that sets many at once:

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(df["body_mass_g"], bins=15)
ax.set(xlabel="Body mass (g)", ylabel="Number of penguins",
       title="Everything in one call")
plt.show()








ax.set(...) accepts any property that has a set_ method, with the prefix dropped. It is a convenient way to keep panel styling to one line, which matters when you are styling six panels in a loop.




9.3.4 Why you should prefer the explicit interface
For one plot, the pyplot style is shorter and perfectly fine. The problem begins the moment there is more than one panel, because “the current Axes” becomes ambiguous — and matplotlib will not warn you when you guess wrong. Consider what happens with two panels:

fig, (ax_left, ax_right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))

ax_left.hist(df["body_mass_g"], bins=15)
ax_left.set_title("Body mass")

ax_right.hist(df["flipper_length_mm"], bins=15)
ax_right.set_title("Flipper length")

plt.title("Where does THIS title go?")
plt.show()








The last plt.title(...) landed on the right-hand panel, because that was the most recently created one and therefore “current”. Worse, it did not just appear in the wrong place — it overwrote that panel’s existing title, so “Flipper length” is now gone. A title meant for the whole figure silently destroyed a panel label instead. Nothing errored; you just get a wrong plot that looks like a finished one.
With the explicit interface the question cannot arise. Each command names its target:

fig, (ax_left, ax_right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))

ax_left.hist(df["body_mass_g"], bins=15)
ax_left.set_title("Body mass")

ax_right.hist(df["flipper_length_mm"], bins=15)
ax_right.set_title("Flipper length")

fig.suptitle("Two measurements, one figure")   # figure-wide, unambiguous
plt.show()








fig.suptitle (“super-title”) is the figure-level title, and because it is a method of fig there is no doubt where it goes.
From here on, this book uses the explicit interface. Three reasons:

It is unambiguous with any number of panels.
It works the same way inside functions and loops, where there is no reliable notion of “current”.
It is what the matplotlib documentation itself now recommends.

The one plt. function we keep using is plt.subplots(), to create the figure in the first place — plus plt.show() at the end.

title: 9  Data Visualization II: Interfaces, Subplots, and Multi-Panel Figures
text:
9.4 Making a grid: plt.subplots()
plt.subplots(nrows, ncols) creates a figure with a grid of panels and returns the figure plus the panels.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
print(type(axes))
print(axes.shape)

<class 'numpy.ndarray'>
(2,)









With more than one panel, the second return value is a NumPy array of Axes objects. You reach a panel by indexing that array. Here the grid is one row by two columns, so axes has shape (2,) and the panels are axes[0] and axes[1]:

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))

sns.histplot(data=df, x="body_mass_g", bins=15, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title("Body mass")

sns.histplot(data=df, x="flipper_length_mm", bins=15, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("Flipper length")

plt.show()








Note the ax= argument on the seaborn calls. That is how you tell a seaborn function which panel to draw into, and we come back to it in detail below.

9.4.1 Indexing: 1D versus 2D
The shape of the axes array follows the shape of your grid, which trips people up constantly:

plt.subplots(1, 2) → shape (2,) → index with one number: axes[0]
plt.subplots(3, 1) → shape (3,) → index with one number: axes[2]
plt.subplots(2, 3) → shape (2, 3) → index with two: axes[0, 2] (row, column)
plt.subplots() → not an array at all — a single Axes, so axes[0] is an error

That last case is the classic bug: fig, axes = plt.subplots() followed by axes[0] raises TypeError: 'Axes' object is not subscriptable. With one panel there is no array to index, which is why the single-panel convention is to name it ax, not axes.
A 2×3 grid, indexed by row and column:

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(13, 6))
print("shape:", axes.shape)

axes[0, 0].set_title("row 0, col 0")
axes[0, 1].set_title("row 0, col 1")
axes[0, 2].set_title("row 0, col 2")
axes[1, 0].set_title("row 1, col 0")
axes[1, 1].set_title("row 1, col 1")
axes[1, 2].set_title("row 1, col 2")

fig.suptitle("An empty 2 × 3 grid, panels labelled by position")
plt.show()

shape: (2, 3)











9.4.2 Useful arguments to plt.subplots()
So far each grid has been built from a row count and a column count alone. A few more arguments to plt.subplots() decide whether the panels can be compared fairly and whether they fit on the figure. The figure below plots the same two measurements for each species, one species per panel:

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 4), sharex=True, sharey=True,
                         layout="constrained")

adelie = df[df["species"] == "Adelie"]
axes[0].scatter(adelie["flipper_length_mm"], adelie["body_mass_g"], s=12)
axes[0].set_title("Adelie")

chinstrap = df[df["species"] == "Chinstrap"]
axes[1].scatter(chinstrap["flipper_length_mm"], chinstrap["body_mass_g"], s=12)
axes[1].set_title("Chinstrap")

gentoo = df[df["species"] == "Gentoo"]
axes[2].scatter(gentoo["flipper_length_mm"], gentoo["body_mass_g"], s=12)
axes[2].set_title("Gentoo")

fig.supxlabel("Flipper length (mm)")
fig.supylabel("Body mass (g)")
fig.suptitle("Flipper length vs. body mass, by species")
plt.show()








The figure uses four arguments beyond the grid shape:







Argument
Effect




figsize=(w, h)
Size of the whole figure in inches. Grids need more room than one plot


sharex=True
All panels use the same x-axis range, and inner tick labels are hidden


sharey=True
Same for the y-axis


layout="constrained"
Automatically space panels so labels and titles don’t collide



sharex / sharey are not cosmetic. When you compare panels side by side, the reader assumes the axes match. If each panel auto-scales to its own data, the same visual distance means a different quantity in each panel, and the comparison is silently invalid. Share the axes whenever the panels show the same variable. Here the shared scales are what let you see at a glance that Gentoo penguins are heavier and have longer flippers: their points sit higher and further right in the same frame.
layout="constrained" fixes overlapping labels. In a grid, one panel’s x-axis label tends to run into the panel below it. Constrained layout computes the spacing for you. You will also see fig.tight_layout() used for this, which is the older approach and works nearly as well; constrained handles shared legends better.
The figure also labels its axes once instead of three times. fig.supxlabel and fig.supylabel are the figure-wide counterparts of ax.set_xlabel and ax.set_ylabel, just as fig.suptitle is the figure-wide title. When the panels share their axes, one label for the whole figure says everything three panel labels would.


9.4.3 Small multiples: one loop, many panels
The species figure repeated the same three lines once per panel, changing only the species. That repetition is the sign to write a loop. A grid of identically built panels, each showing a different variable or group so they can be compared at a glance, is called small multiples.
The loop needs the panels as one sequence, but a 2×2 grid comes back as a 2D array. axes.flat flattens it in reading order — left to right, then top to bottom — and zip pairs each panel with one item from your list. Here the list holds the four measurement columns:

numeric_cols = ["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm",
                "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 7), layout="constrained")

for ax, column in zip(axes.flat, numeric_cols):
    sns.histplot(data=df, x=column, bins=15, ax=ax)
    ax.set_title(column)
    ax.set_xlabel("")

fig.suptitle("Distribution of all four measurements")
plt.show()








Four histograms, one loop, and adding a fifth variable would mean changing only the list and the grid size. Note ax.set_xlabel("") — the column name is already in the panel title, so clearing the axis label removes the duplication.
Here the panels show different variables on different scales, so sharex would be wrong: forcing bill depth (14–22 mm) and body mass (2700–6300 g) onto one x-axis range would make three of the four panels unreadable.

title: 9  Data Visualization II: Interfaces, Subplots, and Multi-Panel Figures
text:
9.5 Uneven layouts
Every grid so far has had panels of equal size. Sometimes one plot is the main point and the others support it, so it deserves more room. plt.subplot_mosaic builds that kind of layout: you draw a picture of it with strings, using a letter per panel, and get back a dictionary keyed by those letters. Repeat a letter to make that panel span the space:

fig, axes = plt.subplot_mosaic(
    """
    AAB
    AAC
    """,
    figsize=(11, 5),
    layout="constrained",
)

print(axes.keys())

sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="flipper_length_mm", y="body_mass_g",
                hue="species", ax=axes["A"])
axes["A"].set_title("Main plot")

sns.histplot(data=df, x="flipper_length_mm", bins=15, ax=axes["B"])
axes["B"].set_title("Flipper length")

sns.histplot(data=df, x="body_mass_g", bins=15, ax=axes["C"])
axes["C"].set_title("Body mass")

fig.suptitle("One big panel with two supporting panels")
plt.show()

dict_keys(['A', 'B', 'C'])









"AAB" / "AAC" describes a 2-row, 3-column grid in which A occupies the whole left 2×2 block while B and C take the right column. Because the panels come back in a dictionary, you refer to them by meaningful letters rather than remembering that the big one is axes[0, 0]. Use . in the string to leave a slot deliberately empty.
You will also meet GridSpec in older code and in the matplotlib documentation. It builds the same layouts by slicing rectangles out of a grid, and the extended practice asks you to try it. The mosaic is the one this course uses.

title: 9  Data Visualization II: Interfaces, Subplots, and Multi-Panel Figures
text:
9.6 Seaborn: axes-level and figure-level functions
Now we can explain something that was postponed in the last chapter. Seaborn’s plotting functions come in two kinds, and the difference is exactly the Figure/Axes distinction we just learned.

9.6.1 Axes-level functions draw into a panel you give them
Every seaborn function used in the last chapter — histplot, scatterplot, boxplot, violinplot, barplot, countplot, kdeplot, heatmap, regplot, stripplot — is axes-level. Each draws onto a single Axes, and each accepts an ax= argument naming which one. With no ax=, it draws into the current Axes, which is why they worked unprompted in the last chapter.
This makes them composable with everything in this chapter:

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4), layout="constrained")

sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="flipper_length_mm", y="body_mass_g",
                hue="species", ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title("scatterplot")

sns.boxplot(data=df, x="species", y="body_mass_g", ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("boxplot")

sns.violinplot(data=df, x="species", y="body_mass_g", ax=axes[2])
axes[2].set_title("violinplot")

fig.suptitle("Three axes-level seaborn functions in one figure")
plt.show()










9.6.2 Figure-level functions create and own the whole figure
Seaborn also offers a smaller set of figure-level functions. Each one wraps a family of axes-level functions and creates its own Figure:








Figure-level function
Wraps
Pick the inner plot with




sns.displot
histplot, kdeplot, ecdfplot
kind="hist", "kde", "ecdf"


sns.relplot
scatterplot, lineplot
kind="scatter", "line"


sns.catplot
boxplot, violinplot, barplot, countplot, stripplot, …
kind="box", "violin", …


sns.lmplot
regplot
(regression only)



In exchange for owning the figure, they give you something the axes-level functions cannot do on their own: automatic faceting. Pass col= or row= and seaborn splits the data by that column and builds one panel per group, laying out the grid itself.

sns.displot(data=df, x="body_mass_g", col="species", bins=15, height=3.5)
plt.show()








One argument, col="species", produced a three-panel figure with shared axes, matching titles, and consistent spacing. Compare that with the manual loop we wrote earlier — this is why figure-level functions exist.
Faceting composes with the visual channels from the last chapter:

sns.relplot(data=df, x="flipper_length_mm", y="body_mass_g",
            col="species", hue="sex", height=3.5)
plt.show()








Now each panel is one species and color distinguishes sex — four variables, cleanly readable, from a single call. And catplot faceting the categorical plots:

sns.catplot(data=df, x="sex", y="body_mass_g", col="species",
            kind="box", height=3.5)
plt.show()








Finally, the promise from the last chapter. We wanted a separate regression line per species and had to loop regplot because it has no hue. lmplot is the figure-level version, and it does have one:

sns.lmplot(data=df, x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", hue="species",
           height=5, aspect=1.2, ci=None)
plt.show()








Three groups, three fitted lines, one call — the Simpson’s paradox figure from the last chapter without the loop. Swap hue for col and you get the same three regressions in three separate panels:

sns.lmplot(data=df, x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", col="species",
           height=3.5, ci=None)
plt.show()










9.6.3 pairplot: every pair of numeric columns at once
Every figure-level function so far built its panels by splitting the rows on a column. sns.pairplot builds them from the columns instead: it draws one panel for every pair of numeric variables, arranged as a grid with one row and one column per variable. It is figure-level in the same way as the others — it creates its own figure, takes no ax=, and sizes each panel with height= — so the whole grid comes from a single call:

sns.pairplot(data=df, hue="species", height=2.2)
plt.show()








Each off-diagonal panel is a scatter plot of the row’s variable against the column’s, so the four penguin measurements give twelve of them. Every pair appears twice, mirrored across the diagonal, which is the same repetition you saw in the correlation table. A variable plotted against itself would be a straight line, so the diagonal panels show each variable’s distribution instead — here a density curve per species, because of hue="species".
A pairplot is the picture behind the correlation heatmap from the last chapter. The heatmap reduces each pair to one number; the pairplot shows the points that number came from, and the two are worth reading together. Take bill depth and body mass. The heatmap gives them a correlation of −0.47, but their panels in the pairplot show three clouds that each slope upward. Within every species, deeper bills go with heavier penguins, and the negative coefficient comes from Gentoo penguins being heavy with shallow bills. That is the Simpson’s paradox pattern from the last chapter, and a single coefficient cannot show it.


9.6.4 The catch: ax= does not work on figure-level functions
Because a figure-level function creates its own Figure, it cannot draw into a panel that already exists. Passing ax= does not raise an error, which makes the mistake easy to miss. Seaborn prints a UserWarning saying that displot is a figure-level function and does not accept ax=, ignores the argument, and draws a separate new figure. The panel you meant to fill stays empty:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)
sns.displot(data=df, x="body_mass_g", ax=axes[0])   # warning; axes[0] stays empty






ImportantThe mistake everyone makes once



This mistake comes up often, and the fix is always to ask whether you need the figure-level function at all:

Putting a seaborn plot into a grid you built? Use the axes-level function with ax=: histplot not displot, scatterplot not relplot, boxplot not catplot, regplot not lmplot.
Want seaborn to build the grid for you, by splitting on a column? Use the figure-level function with col= / row=, and let it own the figure.

A quick way to tell which you are holding: figure-level functions take height and aspect (they size their own figure) and a kind argument; axes-level functions take ax and no kind. Figure-level names also end in -plot after a short prefix — displot, relplot, catplot, lmplot — and are easy to misread as the axes-level names they wrap. displot and histplot are different functions; so are relplot and scatterplot.




9.6.5 Working with what a figure-level function returns
A figure-level call returns a FacetGrid object rather than Axes, and you adjust the result through it:

g = sns.relplot(data=df, x="flipper_length_mm", y="body_mass_g",
                col="species", hue="sex", height=3.5)

g.set_axis_labels("Flipper length (mm)", "Body mass (g)")
g.set_titles("{col_name}")
g.figure.suptitle("Flipper length vs. body mass, by species and sex", y=1.05)
plt.show()















On a FacetGrid g
What it does




g.set_axis_labels(x, y)
Label the x and y axes across all panels


g.set_titles("{col_name}")
Retitle panels; {col_name} is the group’s value


g.figure
The underlying Figure — for suptitle, savefig


g.axes
The array of underlying Axes, if you need one directly


g.axes.flat[0]
The first panel, e.g. to add an annotation


g.savefig("name.png")
Save the figure


col_wrap=3
Wrap a long row of facets onto multiple rows



col_wrap matters when the faceting column has many values. With col= alone, seaborn puts every panel in a single row, which gets uncomfortably wide past four or five groups; col_wrap=3 breaks that row after three panels and continues below. Our penguin columns only have three values each, so there is nothing to wrap here — but remember it the first time you facet on something like a 12-month column.
Faceting on two columns at once, with col= and row=, gives a grid of every combination:

g = sns.displot(data=df, x="body_mass_g", col="island", row="species",
                bins=12, height=2.6)
g.set_titles("{row_name} on {col_name}")
g.figure.suptitle("Body mass by island and species", y=1.03)
plt.show()








Two things to notice.
First, set_titles is doing necessary work. Seaborn’s default title for a two-way facet is the full species = Chinstrap | island = Biscoe, and nine of those across a grid this size run into each other and become unreadable. "{row_name} on {col_name}" substitutes just the group values, giving “Chinstrap on Biscoe”.
Second, four panels are empty, and that is the most informative thing in the figure. Faceting creates a slot for every combination of the two columns, whether or not any rows fall into it, so the blanks show you exactly which combinations do not occur: no Gentoos except on Biscoe, no Chinstraps except on Dream. That is the island/species structure we found with a heatmap in the last chapter, arrived at from a different direction. An empty facet is not a bug in your code — it is data.

title: 9  Data Visualization II: Interfaces, Subplots, and Multi-Panel Figures
text:
9.7 Finishing a multi-panel figure
Whether you built the panels yourself with plt.subplots() or let seaborn build them with col=, what remains is finishing work: one legend instead of three, an inset where points crowd together, tick labels a reader can take in at a glance, and a saved file with nothing cut off. None of these changes what the figure shows. Each one changes how easily a reader gets it.

9.7.1 Sharing a legend across panels
The first finishing job is usually the legend. When every panel uses the same colors, a legend in each one is repeated clutter. The fix is to take the legend entries from one panel, remove the per-panel legends, and attach a single legend to the figure.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4), layout="constrained")

numeric_pairs = [("bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm"),
                 ("flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"),
                 ("bill_length_mm", "body_mass_g")]

for i, (ax, (xcol, ycol)) in enumerate(zip(axes, numeric_pairs)):
    # Let ONLY the first panel build a legend — we harvest it, then delete it.
    sns.scatterplot(data=df, x=xcol, y=ycol, hue="species", ax=ax,
                    legend=(i == 0))
    ax.set_title(f"{xcol} vs {ycol}", fontsize=10)

handles, labels = axes[0].get_legend_handles_labels()
axes[0].get_legend().remove()

fig.legend(handles, labels, title="species",
           loc="outside lower center", ncols=3)

fig.suptitle("Three views of the same penguins, one legend")
plt.show()








The mechanics are worth stepping through, because there is a trap in the obvious version:

legend=(i == 0) passes True for the first panel and False for the other two, so exactly one legend gets built.
get_legend_handles_labels() reads that panel’s legend entries — the colored markers (handles) and the species names (labels).
axes[0].get_legend().remove() then deletes the per-panel legend, now that we have its contents.
fig.legend(handles, labels, ...) attaches them once to the figure.

The trap is step 1. It is tempting to pass legend=False to every panel and then ask for the handles, but a panel that never drew a legend has no labelled artists, so get_legend_handles_labels() returns two empty lists and fig.legend renders a legend box containing nothing but its title. You have to let one panel build a legend in order to steal it.
The loc="outside lower center" position requires layout="constrained", which is one of the places constrained layout beats tight_layout(). ncols=3 lays the three entries out in a row rather than a column, which suits a legend under a wide figure.
If a seaborn function has already drawn a legend you want gone, remove it directly:

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="flipper_length_mm", y="body_mass_g",
                hue="species", ax=ax)
ax.get_legend().remove()
ax.set_title("Legend removed after the fact")
plt.show()










9.7.2 Showing detail with an inset
A finished panel can be right overall but crowded in one region, where the points pile on top of each other. An inset fixes that without a second figure: it puts a small, magnified view of the same data inside the panel, so the main panel keeps the full range while the inset shows the crowded part.
ax.inset_axes([left, bottom, width, height]) creates that small Axes as a child of the panel, positioned in fractions of the parent. [0.58, 0.06, 0.40, 0.29] starts 58% of the way across and 6% up, and takes 40% of the width and 29% of the height. Because the numbers are relative to the parent, the inset stays put when the surrounding layout changes.
ax.indicate_inset_zoom() then draws the rectangle marking the magnified region and the lines connecting it to the inset. Without it, the reader has to work out the relationship from the axis numbers alone.
An inset also needs somewhere to sit where it covers nothing. This scatter has no penguins with long flippers and low body mass, so its bottom-right corner is free, and widening the limits a little past the data with ax.set(xlim=..., ylim=...) makes that corner roomier without moving a single point.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 5), layout="constrained")

sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="flipper_length_mm", y="body_mass_g", hue="species",
                alpha=0.7, ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel("Flipper length (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
ax.set_title("Where the points pile up, an inset can show the detail")

# Widen the limits past the data, clearing a corner for the inset.
ax.set(xlim=(168, 246), ylim=(2300, 6500))

# A child Axes, placed in fractions of the parent panel.
zoom = ax.inset_axes([0.58, 0.06, 0.40, 0.29])
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="flipper_length_mm", y="body_mass_g", hue="species",
                alpha=0.7, legend=False, ax=zoom)
zoom.set(xlim=(185, 200), ylim=(3000, 4200), xlabel="", ylabel="")
zoom.tick_params(labelsize=7)

ax.indicate_inset_zoom(zoom, edgecolor="gray")
plt.show()








Two details of craft. Put the inset where the data is not: the magnified view sits in the empty corner, so it hides nothing — and that includes the inset’s own tick labels, which are drawn outside its frame and will cover points if you place it too tightly. Widening the limits is the cheap way to clear that space. If no corner can be freed, the region deserves its own panel instead.
Keep the inset’s ticks. The temptation is to strip them for tidiness, but an inset has a different scale from its parent and those numbers are the only thing saying so. Here legend=False drops the duplicate legend and the axis labels are dropped because the parent already names both variables — the tick numbers stay.


9.7.3 Formatting tick labels
The legend and the inset add things to a figure. The next finishing step changes how a panel’s own numbers read. Matplotlib writes tick labels straight from the data, which gives you 6000 where a reader expects 6,000, and 0.44 where they expect 44%. The fix lives on the axis objects ax.xaxis and ax.yaxis — another place where having the object in hand is what makes the adjustment possible.
set_major_formatter accepts a format string in which {x} stands for the tick value. '{x:,.0f}' is a thousands separator with no decimals; '{x:.0%}' turns a proportion into a percentage.

fig, (ax_mass, ax_share) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4), layout="constrained")

sns.histplot(data=df, x="body_mass_g", bins=20, ax=ax_mass)
ax_mass.xaxis.set_major_formatter('{x:,.0f}')
ax_mass.set(xlabel="Body mass (g)", title="A thousands separator on the x-axis")

shares = df["species"].value_counts(normalize=True)
ax_share.bar(shares.index, shares.values, color="steelblue")
ax_share.yaxis.set_major_formatter('{x:.0%}')
ax_share.set(ylabel="Share of penguins", title="Proportions read as percentages")

plt.show()








The right-hand panel holds proportions — value_counts(normalize=True), from Pandas Fundamentals — so the values behind the bars are 0.442, 0.360, and 0.198. The formatter is what makes them read as the percentages a caption would quote, and the data itself is untouched: format for the reader rather than by rewriting your numbers.
Two adjustments you will reach for on the same figures: ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45) when category names overlap, and ax.set_xticks([...]) when you want to choose the tick positions yourself instead of accepting matplotlib’s.


9.7.4 Saving a multi-panel figure
The last finishing step is writing the figure to a file. With the figure in a variable, save it with fig.savefig:

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4), layout="constrained")
sns.histplot(data=df, x="body_mass_g", bins=15, ax=axes[0])
sns.histplot(data=df, x="flipper_length_mm", bins=15, ax=axes[1])
fig.suptitle("Saved to a file")

fig.savefig("penguin_panels.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()








Three points, two of which bit us in the last chapter:

fig.savefig, not plt.savefig. With several figures in flight, plt.savefig saves whichever is current — name the one you mean.
Save before plt.show(). plt.show() closes out the figure, so saving afterwards writes a blank image. In the explicit interface this is less dangerous, since fig still refers to the figure, but keep the habit.
bbox_inches="tight" crops surrounding whitespace and, importantly, stops a suptitle or an outside legend from being cut off. dpi=300 is a reasonable resolution for print.

For a figure-level seaborn plot, save through the FacetGrid: g.savefig("name.png"), or equivalently g.figure.savefig(...).

9.10.1 Mosaic against GridSpec
GridSpec is matplotlib’s older tool for uneven layouts. Instead of drawing the layout as a string, you create an empty figure with fig = plt.figure(), divide it into a grid with gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 3), and claim each panel by slicing that grid: fig.add_subplot(gs[:, 0:2]) is a panel spanning every row and the first two columns. 9.10.2 Empty Panels, and What They Tell You

9.10.3 One Legend for the Whole Figure

9.10.4 Two Y-Axes, and Whether to Use Them
Two variables with different units sometimes seem to belong on one panel. ax.twinx() returns a second Axes that shares ax’s x-axis but has its own y-axis on the right, so each variable gets its own scale. title: 9  Data Visualization II: Interfaces, Subplots, and Multi-Panel Figures
text:
9.11 Before You Move On
The habit to carry forward is naming the thing you draw into. A single quick plot can go through plt.* and land wherever pyplot puts it, but as soon as a figure has more than one panel, every command needs an address: ax for a panel, fig for the whole canvas. Axes-level seaborn functions take that address through ax=; figure-level ones refuse it, because they build the figure themselves.
The other habit is making the panels comparable. A grid invites the reader to compare its panels, so share the axes when the panels show the same variable, and give the figure enough room that none of it is cramped.
For any multi-panel figure you make or read, you should be able to answer four questions:

What is one panel, and what changes from panel to panel?
Are the axes shared, and if not, could a reader mistake the panels for comparable?
Which commands addressed a panel, and which addressed the whole figure?
Did seaborn build these panels, or did you — and does the function you called accept ax=?

Continue to Data Cleaning, where the messy realities you have been plotting around — missing values, duplicated records, extreme values — become the subject rather than a footnote.
References: matplotlib quick start, figure anatomy, plt.subplots, subplot_mosaic, constrained layout, seaborn figure-level versus axes-level functions, FacetGrid, and pairplot.

title: 10  Data Cleaning
text:
10.1 Set Up Your Chapter Files
The last two chapters drew pictures of a dataset that was already in good shape. Data Visualization I warned you that every plotting library drops missing values without saying so, and asked you to know how many observations a plot left out. That warning is where this chapter begins: real data arrives with gaps, with the same record entered twice, and with values so far from the rest that they deserve a second look.
Cleaning is the work of finding those problems, deciding what each one means, and fixing it in a way you can defend. The deciding is the hard part. A missing value can be dropped, filled from its own column, or filled from related rows and columns, and the right choice depends on why it is missing. An extreme value can be a measurement error to correct or a real observation to keep. Every fix changes the data you analyse afterwards, so this chapter measures what each fix costs instead of taking it on trust.
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:
Complete the practice activity after the worked examples.
Download the Data Cleaning practice kit. Extract stat303-data-cleaning inside the chapters folder of your stat303-1 course folder, open stat303-1 in VS Code, and select the course environment. The terminal opens in stat303-1, so move it into the kit with cd chapters and then cd stat303-data-cleaning before you render the activity.
Run data_cleaning_examples.ipynb for the lesson and complete activity10.ipynb for your own activity report, with stat303-data-cleaning as the notebook working folder. Every file is read with a relative path such as "data/GDP_missing_data.csv", so the notebooks find their data only when that folder is the working folder.

title: 10  Data Cleaning
text:
10.4 Why values go missing
Counting tells you how much is missing. Before choosing a fix, ask why, because the reason decides whether a fix is safe. Statisticians sort the reasons into three mechanisms:









Mechanism
What it means
GDP example
Dropping or a simple fill is…




MCAR — missing completely at random
Missingness has nothing to do with any value, observed or not
A file was corrupted and lost random rows
Safe: what remains is still a fair sample


MAR — missing at random
Missingness depends on other columns you can see
Countries in one continent report less often
Biased, but other columns can correct it


MNAR — missing not at random
Missingness depends on the missing value itself
The poorest countries are the ones that do not report GDP
Biased, and the data alone cannot fix it



The names are confusing — “missing at random” is not the safe one — so remember the idea rather than the label. MCAR means the gaps are like a coin flip. MAR means the gaps follow a pattern you can see in other columns, so a fill that uses those columns can undo the damage. MNAR means the gaps follow the very values you are missing, and any fill will be wrong in a predictable direction.
You cannot prove which mechanism you have from the data, but you can look for evidence. If the countries missing GDP are concentrated in one continent, the gaps are at least not MCAR. Keep the question in mind for every fill that follows: a method that uses related columns can help with MAR, while nothing in this chapter rescues MNAR.

title: 10  Data Cleaning
text:
10.5 Drop missing data
The bluntest fix is to throw away anything incomplete. You used dropna(subset=[...]) in the workflow chapter to drop rows missing one particular column. Called with no arguments, dropna() drops every row with any missing value:

print("rows before:", len(gdp))
print("rows after dropna():", len(gdp.dropna()))

rows before: 155
rows after dropna(): 42


From 155 countries to 42: over two thirds of the data gone, including thousands of perfectly good values that happened to share a row with one gap. The culprit is mostly a single column. contraception is missing for 71 countries, so almost every row has some gap. A column missing half its values is a weak basis for filling anything, so the better move is to drop that column and keep the rows:

gdp = gdp.drop(columns="contraception")

print("columns left:", gdp.shape[1])
print("rows after dropna():", len(gdp.dropna()))

columns left: 11
rows after dropna(): 88


Dropping one column brings dropna() back to 88 rows. Note that drop(columns=...) returns a new DataFrame, so the result is assigned back to gdp; nothing changes in place.
dropna() has three arguments that make it less blunt:








Argument
Effect
Here




subset=["gdpPerCapita"]
Only look for gaps in these columns
Keeps the 145 rows that have GDP


how="all"
Drop a row only if every value is missing
Drops nothing; no row is entirely empty


thresh=10
Keep a row only if it has at least 10 non-missing values
Keeps 143 of 155 rows



Even 88 rows means discarding 67 countries over a handful of gaps each. Filling the gaps instead keeps those countries, which is what the rest of this section is about.

title: 10  Data Cleaning
text:
10.6 Fill missing values
Filling a missing value is called imputation, and every imputation is a guess. The question is how good the guess is, and here, unusually, we can measure it. For the 10 countries missing GDP per capita, gdp_complete holds the true values, so any fill can be scored against them.
The score is the root mean squared error (RMSE): square each error, average the squares, take the square root. It is in the same units as the data — dollars of GDP per capita here — and smaller is better. The function below computes it for a filled GDP column and draws each guess against the truth, so every method in this section gets the same report:

gdp_missing = gdp["gdpPerCapita"].isna()       # the 10 rows we will be guessing
true_gdp = gdp_complete.loc[gdp_missing, "gdpPerCapita"]

def score_fill(filled_gdp, method):
    """Plot filled GDP against the truth for the missing rows, and return the RMSE."""
    guesses = filled_gdp[gdp_missing]
    rmse = np.sqrt(((guesses - true_gdp) ** 2).mean())

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.5), layout="constrained")
    ax.scatter(true_gdp, guesses, s=50)
    ax.axline((0, 0), slope=1, color="gray", linestyle="--", label="perfect guess")
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter("${x:,.0f}")
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter("${x:,.0f}")
    top = max(true_gdp.max(), guesses.max()) * 1.05     # same range on both axes
    ax.set(xlim=(0, top), ylim=(0, top),
           xlabel="True GDP per capita", ylabel="Filled GDP per capita",
           title=f"{method}: RMSE ${rmse:,.0f}")
    ax.legend(loc="upper left")
    plt.show()
    return rmse

gdp_missing is a Boolean mask, so filled_gdp[gdp_missing] keeps only the guessed rows. ax.axline((0, 0), slope=1) draws the line where a guess equals the truth: points on it are perfect, and the farther a point sits from it, the worse that guess. Both axes share one range so that line is a true diagonal, and the tick formatter is the one from Data Visualization II.

10.6.1 Fill with the column mean
The simplest guess for a missing number is the typical value of its column. fillna(value) replaces every NaN in a Series with value:

mean_gdp = gdp["gdpPerCapita"].mean()
print(f"mean GDP per capita: ${mean_gdp:,.0f}")

rmse_mean = score_fill(gdp["gdpPerCapita"].fillna(mean_gdp), "Column mean")

mean GDP per capita: $24,193









Every missing country gets the same $24,193, so the points form a horizontal line. A rich country and a poor one receive the same guess, which is why the RMSE is about $30,800.
Filling with the median instead — fillna(gdp["gdpPerCapita"].median()) — is the usual advice for skewed data like GDP, and it does give a more typical value ($15,184). It scores slightly worse here, about $32,100, because these particular missing countries are not typical. Neither statistic can tell one country from another.
A column-wide fill also shrinks the column’s spread, since every gap becomes the same middle value. For a categorical column, the equivalent guess is the most common category, df["col"].mode()[0].


10.6.2 Fill with a group mean
GDP per capita varies enormously by continent, which a box plot shows at once:

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5), layout="constrained")
sns.boxplot(data=gdp, x="continent", y="gdpPerCapita", ax=ax)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter("${x:,.0f}")
ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="GDP per capita")
plt.show()








A missing European country is much more likely to be near Europe’s typical GDP than near the world’s. Filling each gap with its own continent’s mean uses the continent column to make a better guess, which is exactly the kind of fill that can correct MAR missingness.
That needs a mean for each continent, and the tool for “split the rows into groups, then compute something per group” is groupby(). The full story waits for Data Grouping and Aggregation; here you need only its simplest form. gdp.groupby("continent")["gdpPerCapita"].mean() splits the rows by continent and returns one mean per continent, skipping missing values as every pandas statistic does:

gdp.groupby("continent")["gdpPerCapita"].mean().round(0)

continent
Africa            7638.0
Asia             25923.0
Europe           45455.0
North America    19625.0
Oceania          15386.0
South America    15361.0
Name: gdpPerCapita, dtype: float64


That is one number per continent, six in all. To fill a column you need one number per row: each country’s own continent mean, lined up with the country. Replacing .mean() with .transform("mean") does exactly that. It computes the same group means, then hands each row the mean of its group, so the result has 155 values in the original row order:

continent_mean = gdp.groupby("continent")["gdpPerCapita"].transform("mean")
print(continent_mean.head())

rmse_group = score_fill(gdp["gdpPerCapita"].fillna(continent_mean), "Continent mean")

0    25922.750000
1     7638.178571
2    15360.909091
3    25922.750000
4    15385.857143
Name: gdpPerCapita, dtype: float64









fillna() accepts a Series as well as a single value. It fills each gap from the entry at the same row label, so each country gets its continent’s mean. The guesses now differ by continent and the RMSE drops to about $25,500.


10.6.3 Fill from a related column
A different way to use other columns is to predict the missing value from one that is strongly related to it. corrwith() correlates every numeric column with GDP per capita:

gdp.select_dtypes("number").corrwith(gdp["gdpPerCapita"]).round(2)

economicActivityFemale    0.08
lifeMale                  0.58
infantMortality          -0.57
gdpPerCapita              1.00
economicActivityMale     -0.13
illiteracyMale           -0.48
illiteracyFemale         -0.45
lifeFemale                0.62
dtype: float64


Female life expectancy has the strongest correlation, 0.62. The idea is to fit a straight line predicting GDP from lifeFemale — the same least-squares line seaborn’s regplot drew in Data Visualization I — and read each missing country’s GDP off that line.
np.polyfit(x, y, 1) fits that line and returns its slope and intercept; the 1 asks for a straight line. It cannot handle NaN, so it is fitted only on the countries that have both values:

both_known = gdp["lifeFemale"].notna() & gdp["gdpPerCapita"].notna()
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(gdp.loc[both_known, "lifeFemale"],
                              gdp.loc[both_known, "gdpPerCapita"], 1)
print(f"GDP per capita ≈ {intercept:,.0f} + {slope:,.0f} × lifeFemale")

predicted_gdp = intercept + slope * gdp["lifeFemale"]
rmse_regression = score_fill(gdp["gdpPerCapita"].fillna(predicted_gdp), "Regression on lifeFemale")

GDP per capita ≈ -79,453 + 1,473 × lifeFemale









Each extra year of female life expectancy predicts about $1,473 more GDP per capita. The RMSE, about $25,600, is close to the continent mean’s: one strongly related column carries roughly as much information as the continent does. This works only because lifeFemale is present for every country missing GDP; a predictor with its own gaps would leave those rows unfilled.


10.6.4 Fill from the nearest neighbours
The last two fills each used one other column. K-nearest-neighbour (KNN) imputation uses all of them at once: to fill a gap in one country, find the K countries most similar to it across every other numeric column, and average their values.
“Most similar” means smallest Euclidean distance, the straight-line distance you learned in geometry, computed across all the columns a pair of rows both have. A toy array of four rows and three columns shows the mechanics:

toy = np.array([[1, 2, np.nan],
                [3, 4, 3],
                [np.nan, 6, 5],
                [8, 8, 7]])

nan_euclidean_distances(toy)

array([[ 0.        ,  3.46410162,  6.92820323, 11.29158979],
       [ 3.46410162,  0.        ,  3.46410162,  7.54983444],
       [ 6.92820323,  3.46410162,  0.        ,  3.46410162],
       [11.29158979,  7.54983444,  3.46410162,  0.        ]])


Entry \((i, j)\) is the distance from row \(i\) to row \(j\), counting rows from 0 as NumPy does. nan_euclidean_distances from scikit-learn skips any coordinate where either row is missing and scales the result up to make up for it. Row 0 is closest to row 1 (3.46), then row 2 (6.93). Row 2 is equally close to rows 1 and 3 (3.46 each).
KNNImputer does the averaging. Like every scikit-learn tool, it is used in two steps: create the object with its settings, then call fit_transform() on the data:

imputer = KNNImputer(n_neighbors=2)
imputer.fit_transform(toy)

array([[1. , 2. , 4. ],
       [3. , 4. , 3. ],
       [5.5, 6. , 5. ],
       [8. , 8. , 7. ]])


With n_neighbors=2, each gap is the mean of the two nearest rows that have a value in that column. Row 0’s missing third value is 4.0, the mean of rows 1 and 2 (3 and 5). Row 2’s missing first value is 5.5, the mean of rows 1 and 3 (3 and 8).
On the real data, one more step matters. Distance adds up differences across columns, and GDP per capita runs into the tens of thousands while life expectancy runs from about 40 to 80. Unscaled, GDP alone would decide who counts as a neighbour. MinMaxScaler rescales each column to run from 0 to 1, so every column gets an equal say; it remembers each column’s original range, so inverse_transform() can convert back to dollars afterwards:

numeric = gdp.select_dtypes("number")          # the eight measurement columns

scaler = MinMaxScaler()
scaled = scaler.fit_transform(numeric)         # every column now runs from 0 to 1

imputer = KNNImputer(n_neighbors=3)
filled_scaled = imputer.fit_transform(scaled)  # gaps filled from 3 nearest countries

filled = pd.DataFrame(scaler.inverse_transform(filled_scaled),
                      columns=numeric.columns, index=numeric.index)

rmse_knn = score_fill(filled["gdpPerCapita"], "KNN, K = 3")








Both scikit-learn steps return plain NumPy arrays, so the last step wraps the result back into a DataFrame with the original column names and row labels. The RMSE falls to about $16,800, the best so far, because KNN finds countries that resemble the missing one on every measurement at once. It also fills the gaps in the other seven columns in the same pass.
The choice \(K = 3\) matters more than it looks. On this data, \(K = 2\) gives about $21,400 and \(K = 5\) about $23,500, so K is a setting to choose carefully rather than a detail. Choosing it properly uses a technique called cross-validation, which comes in the next course of the sequence.


10.6.5 Forward fill, and when not to use it
ffill() fills each gap with the value in the row above it (bfill() uses the row below). For data in a meaningful order, such as daily temperatures, yesterday’s value is a sensible guess for a missing today. Our countries are in alphabetical order, which has nothing to do with GDP:

rmse_ffill = score_fill(gdp["gdpPerCapita"].ffill(), "Forward fill")








Forward fill gives the worst result of all, about $34,800: worse than guessing the mean, because the neighbour in alphabetical order is no guide to a country’s wealth. It also cannot fill a gap in the very first row, since there is nothing above it; Afghanistan’s missing illiteracyMale survives a forward fill of the whole table.


10.6.6 Compare the fills

pd.Series({
    "Forward fill": rmse_ffill,
    "Column mean": rmse_mean,
    "Regression on lifeFemale": rmse_regression,
    "Continent mean": rmse_group,
    "KNN, K = 3": rmse_knn,
}).round(0).rename("RMSE")

Forward fill                34844.0
Column mean                 30794.0
Regression on lifeFemale    25570.0
Continent mean              25473.0
KNN, K = 3                  16804.0
Name: RMSE, dtype: float64


The ranking follows how much information each method uses. Forward fill uses an irrelevant ordering, the column mean uses only the column itself, the next two each add one related variable, and KNN uses every column at once. That is the general lesson, but the exact order is specific to this data. On another dataset a group mean can beat KNN, which is why the comparison is worth running whenever you can.
Every fill shares one limit: it invents values that look like real data. Whatever you choose, record which values were filled and how, so a reader can judge how much the results depend on your guesses.

title: 10  Data Cleaning
text:
10.7 Find and remove duplicates
A duplicate is the same record appearing more than once. Duplicates come from data entry errors, from combining files that overlap, or from a system that saved a record twice, and they are dangerous because they look like real data: a duplicated student is counted twice in every total and average.
A small table of student records, with some entered twice, shows the tools:

title: 10  Data Cleaning
text:
10.8 Find and handle outliers
An outlier is an observation far from the rest of the data. Outliers matter because the mean, the standard deviation, and a fitted line are all pulled toward them, so a few extreme values can change the story a summary tells.
This section uses data on 777 US colleges from An Introduction to Statistical Learning. The first column holds the college names, so index_col=0 uses it as the row labels, as in Reading Data:

college = pd.read_csv("data/College.csv", index_col=0)
print(college.shape)
college[["Private", "Apps", "Enroll", "Expend", "Grad.Rate"]].head()

(777, 18)









Private
Apps
Enroll
Expend
Grad.Rate




Abilene Christian University
Yes
1660

7041
60


Adelphi University
Yes
2186

Yes
1428

Expend is instructional expenditure per student, in dollars, and Grad.Rate is the graduation rate as a percentage.

10.8.1 See them
A box plot marks outliers directly: the points beyond the whiskers. A histogram shows the same values as a long, thin tail:

fig, (ax_box, ax_hist) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4), layout="constrained")

sns.boxplot(data=college, y="Expend", ax=ax_box)
ax_box.yaxis.set_major_formatter("${x:,.0f}")
ax_box.set(ylabel="Expenditure per student", title="Box plot")

sns.histplot(data=college, x="Expend", bins=30, ax=ax_hist)
ax_hist.xaxis.set_major_formatter("${x:,.0f}")
ax_hist.set(xlabel="Expenditure per student", title="Histogram")

plt.show()








Most colleges spend between about $5,000 and $15,000 per student, and a tail of colleges spends far more, up to Johns Hopkins at $56,233. A picture tells you outliers exist; to work with them you need a rule that flags each one.


10.8.2 Flag them with a rule
The z-score rule. A z-score measures how many standard deviations a value is from the mean, \(z = (x - \bar{x}) / s\). A common convention flags values with \(|z| > 3\). stats.zscore() from SciPy computes z-scores for a whole column:

z = stats.zscore(college["Expend"])
z_outlier = np.abs(z) > 3
print("z-score outliers:", z_outlier.sum())

z-score outliers: 16


stats.zscore() returns a NumPy array, so np.abs() takes the absolute value and the comparison gives a Boolean array you can sum. It divides by the standard deviation with ddof=0, the NumPy default from NumPy Fundamentals; computing (x - x.mean()) / x.std(ddof=0) by hand gives the same values.
The IQR rule. This is the rule the box plot used. With \(Q1\) and \(Q3\) the 25th and 75th percentiles and \(IQR = Q3 - Q1\), anything below \(Q1 - 1.5 \times IQR\) or above \(Q3 + 1.5 \times IQR\) is an outlier. These boundaries are called Tukey’s fences. quantile() gives the percentiles:

q1, q3 = college["Expend"].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
iqr = q3 - q1
lower, upper = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
print(f"fences: ${lower:,.0f} to ${upper:,.0f}")

iqr_outlier = (college["Expend"] < lower) | (college["Expend"] > upper)
print("IQR outliers:", iqr_outlier.sum())

fences: $632 to $16,948
IQR outliers: 48


The IQR rule flags 48 colleges and the z-score rule only 16. The difference comes from the right skew. The z-score uses the mean and standard deviation, and the long tail inflates both, so a value has to be very extreme to reach \(|z| > 3\). The quartiles barely move with the tail, so the IQR fences stay close to the bulk of the data.









Rule
Built on
Assumes
Flags




z-score
Mean and standard deviation
Roughly bell-shaped data
Fewer, more extreme values


IQR
Quartiles
Nothing about shape
More values; suits skewed data



Neither number is the “true” count of outliers. A rule only nominates candidates; deciding what to do with them comes next.


10.8.3 Ask whether it is an error
Before handling an outlier, ask whether the value is possible. The graduation rates show the difference:

college["Grad.Rate"].describe()

count    777.00000
mean      65.46332
std       17.17771
min       10.00000
25%       53.00000
50%       65.00000
75%       78.00000
max      118.00000
Name: Grad.Rate, dtype: float64



college.loc[college["Grad.Rate"] > 100, ["Grad.Rate"]]








Grad.Rate




Cazenovia College
118







A graduation rate of 118% is impossible, so Cazenovia College’s value is a data error, not an extreme. Capping it at some fence would still leave an invented number. The honest fix is to mark it as missing, which turns it into the problem the first half of this chapter solved:
college.loc[college["Grad.Rate"] > 100, "Grad.Rate"] = np.nan
Johns Hopkins spending $56,233 per student is the opposite case: extreme, but entirely plausible for a research university. Removing it would delete a real fact about American colleges. Errors get corrected or set to missing; real extremes get a deliberate choice from the methods below.


10.8.4 Handle them
Four common ways to handle real outliers, each applied to Expend with the IQR fences:

expend = college["Expend"]

removed = expend[~iqr_outlier]                         # drop flagged colleges
capped = expend.clip(lower, upper)                     # pull them back to the fences
median_filled = expend.mask(iqr_outlier, removed.median())   # replace with a typical value
logged = np.log(expend)                                # compress the whole scale

pd.DataFrame({
    "rows": [len(expend), len(removed), len(capped), len(median_filled)],
    "mean": [expend.mean(), removed.mean(), capped.mean(), median_filled.mean()],
    "std": [expend.std(), removed.std(), capped.std(), median_filled.std()],
}, index=["original", "removed", "capped", "median-filled"]).round(0)








rows
mean
std




original

clip(lower, upper), from Pandas Intermediate, moves any value outside the range to the nearest fence; this is also called winsorizing. mask(condition, value) replaces the values where the condition is True.
All three shrink the standard deviation from about $5,200 to under $3,400, and all three lower the mean. That is the point of handling outliers, and also the danger: the cleaned column describes colleges that spend less, and vary less, than the real ones do.








Method
Keeps every row
Cost




Remove
No
Loses the colleges, and anything else they recorded

Yes
Invents a boundary value; real extremes look ordinary


Replace with the median
Yes
Invents a typical value; spread shrinks most


Log transform
Yes
Changes the units, so results must be read on a log scale



The log transform is different in kind. It keeps every value and its order, but compresses large values more than small ones, so the skewness of Expend drops from about 3.5 to 0.8. It suits strictly positive, right-skewed quantities such as money, and np.log1p() handles columns that contain zeros.
Whichever you choose, report it: how many values were flagged, by which rule, and what was done to them.

title: 10  Data Cleaning
text:
10.9 Summary Cheat Sheet
Find missing values.



Goal
Code




Count per column
df.isna().sum()


Percent per column
df.isna().mean() * 100


Non-missing counts
df.describe() (count row), df.info()



Drop or fill.







Goal
Code




Drop rows with any gap
df.dropna()


Only check some columns
df.dropna(subset=["col"])


Keep rows with at least n values
df.dropna(thresh=n)


Drop a mostly empty column
df.drop(columns="col")


Fill with one value
df["col"].fillna(df["col"].mean())


Fill with each row’s group mean
df["col"].fillna(df.groupby("g")["col"].transform("mean"))


Fill from a related column
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x, y, 1) on complete rows


Fill from nearest neighbours
MinMaxScaler, then KNNImputer(n_neighbors=k).fit_transform(...)


Fill from the row above
df.ffill() — only for ordered data


Score a fill against the truth
np.sqrt(((guess - truth) ** 2).mean())



Duplicates.







Goal
Code




Count repeated rows
df.duplicated().sum()


Show every copy
df[df.duplicated(keep=False)]


Check one key column
df.duplicated(subset=["id"])


Remove repeats
df.drop_duplicates(subset=..., keep="first" / "last" / False)



Outliers.







Goal
Code




z-scores
z = stats.zscore(s); flag np.abs(z) > 3


IQR fences
q1, q3 = s.quantile([0.25, 0.75]); q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr


Impossible value → missing
df.loc[condition, "col"] = np.nan


Cap at the fences
s.clip(lower, upper)


Replace flagged values
s.mask(flags, value)


Compress a right skew
np.log(s) or np.log1p(s)



The rule to remember: measure what a fix costs before you trust it.

text:

title: 10  Data Cleaning
text:
10.12 Before You Move On
The habit to carry forward is measuring a fix before you trust it. Dropping rows, filling gaps, removing repeats, and capping extremes each change the data every later step will see, and each one can be checked: how many rows it removed, how far its guesses were from the truth, how much it moved a mean or a standard deviation.
The other habit is asking what a problem means before choosing a fix. A gap may follow a pattern you can see in other columns, or one you cannot. A repeated record may be a copy or a correction. An extreme value may be an error or a fact. The code for every fix in this chapter is a line or two; the judgement around it is the work.
For any dataset you clean, you should be able to answer five questions:

How many values were missing in each column, and why might they be missing?
What did you drop, and how much data did that cost?
How did you fill the rest, and how good were those guesses?
Were any records duplicated, and how did you decide which copy to keep?
Which values did you flag as outliers, and which of them were errors?

Continue to Data Preparation, where clean data is reshaped into the form an analysis needs.
References: pandas: working with missing data, DataFrame.dropna, Series.fillna, DataFrame.groupby, DataFrame.duplicated, DataFrame.drop_duplicates, np.polyfit, scikit-learn KNNImputer, MinMaxScaler, and SciPy stats.zscore.

title: 11  Data Preparation
text:
11.1 Set Up Your Chapter Files
Data Cleaning fixed what was wrong with the data: gaps, repeats, and values that could not be true. Clean data is not always in the form an analysis needs, though. A comparison may be clearer between a few groups than across hundreds of distinct values. A method may need numbers where the data has categories. Two columns may need to be put on a common scale before they can be combined fairly.
This chapter is about reshaping clean data for the question you want to ask, without changing what it says. Each preparation step is a choice — how many groups and where their edges fall, how to turn a category into numbers, which columns to rescale — and each choice changes what the next step can see. The habit to build is checking the result of every choice before you trust it.
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:
Complete the practice activity after the worked examples.
Download the Data Preparation practice kit. Extract stat303-data-preparation inside the chapters folder of your stat303-1 course folder, open stat303-1 in VS Code, and select the course environment. The data is read with the relative path "data/College.csv", so the notebooks find it only when that folder is the working folder.
