title: 11  Data Preparation
text:
11.3 Bin a numeric column
A scatter plot answers the spending question for every college at once, and with 777 noisy points the answer is hard to read:

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5), layout="constrained")
sns.scatterplot(data=college, x="Expend", y="Grad.Rate", alpha=0.5, ax=ax)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter("${x:,.0f}")
ax.set(xlabel="Expenditure per student", ylabel="Graduation rate (%)")
plt.show()








Each college is one point, and Expend alone has hundreds of distinct values. The standard way to make a comparison like this readable is to bin the column.

11.3.1 What binning is, and why it helps
Data binning groups the values of a numeric column into a few intervals, called bins, and records which bin each value falls into instead of the value itself. Think of it as sorting a long list of numbers into a few labelled jars. Binning simplifies a column so that patterns become visible and comparisons become easy to state.
Why bin?

Easier interpretation. Instead of hundreds of distinct values, you summarize a handful of groups. Rather than every possible age, a report might use the age groups “under 20”, “20 to 30”, “30 to 40”, and “40 and over”.
Targeted decisions. Groups support decisions made group by group. A doctor may recommend different treatments for children, adults, and older adults, each defined by an age bin.
Less noise. Grouping smooths random fluctuation. Daily sales may jump around, while weekly or monthly totals show the trend.

Binning in the real world.

Tax brackets. Income is binned into ranges that are taxed at different rates. For a single filer in 2024, the first $11,600 of taxable income is taxed at 10%, the part from $11,601 to $47,150 at 12%, and the part above that at 22% or more.
Customer segments. A credit card company may bin customers into high, medium, and low spenders and market to each group differently.
Medical guidelines. Vaccine recommendations often depend on age bins, such as under 12, 12 to 18, 18 to 65, and over 65.







Tax brackets bin a taxable income of $50,000 into three ranges, each taxed at its own rate.







A bar chart of counts by binned age: four age groups replace every distinct age.





Here, binning Expend into low, medium, and high spending lets you compare one summary per group instead of reading a cloud of points. The price is detail: once a college is “medium”, the exact dollar figure is gone. That makes the choice of bins, how many and where their edges fall, the important decision. There are three common ways to make it, and the rest of this section works through each:









Method
pandas
Bins have
Suits




Equal-width
pd.cut(s, k)
The same width, any count
Values spread fairly evenly


Equal-count (quantile)
pd.qcut(s, k)
The same count, any width
Skewed columns; groups you want to compare


Custom
pd.cut(s, bins=[...])
Edges you choose
Thresholds that mean something





11.3.2 Equal-width bins with cut()
pd.cut(column, 3) divides the range of a column, from its minimum to its maximum, into 3 intervals of equal width, and returns which interval each value falls into. value_counts(sort=False) lists the intervals in order with their counts:

pd.cut(college["Expend"], 3).value_counts(sort=False)

Expend
(3132.953, 20868.333]     751
(20868.333, 38550.667]     21
(38550.667, 56233.0]        5
Name: count, dtype: int64


Each interval is written (left, right]: the round bracket means the left edge is excluded and the square bracket means the right edge is included, so every value belongs to exactly one bin. (The lowest edge sits slightly below the minimum so that the minimum is included.)
The widths are equal, about $17,700 each, but the counts are not: 751 colleges in the first bin, 21 in the second, and 5 in the third. Expend is strongly right-skewed, as Data Cleaning showed, so a few very high spenders stretch the range and the top two bins cover almost no one. Comparing group means anyway gives a misleading answer:

width_level = pd.cut(college["Expend"], 3, labels=["Low", "Medium", "High"])
college.groupby(width_level)["Grad.Rate"].mean().round(1)

Expend
Low       64.6
Medium    90.6
High      83.2
Name: Grad.Rate, dtype: float64


labels= names the bins in order, from lowest to highest. The groupby(...).mean() pattern is the one introduced in Data Cleaning, here grouping by the bin each college falls into.
Read naively, the table says medium spenders graduate the most students. But “medium” and “high” are 21 and 5 colleges; a single unusual school moves either mean by several points. Always check the counts before comparing bins. Equal-width bins suit columns whose values are spread fairly evenly. For a skewed column they put nearly everything in one bin.


11.3.3 Equal-count bins with qcut()
pd.qcut(column, 3) does the opposite: it places the edges at the column’s quantiles, so each bin holds roughly the same number of rows. Three equal-count bins are called tertiles:

college["expend_level"] = pd.qcut(college["Expend"], 3, labels=["Low", "Medium", "High"])
college["expend_level"].value_counts(sort=False)

expend_level
Low       259
Medium    259
High      259
Name: count, dtype: int64


Each bin now holds 259 colleges. The edges fall at about $7,334 and $9,682, the 33rd and 67th percentiles. Drawing both sets of edges on the distribution shows the difference between the two methods:

width_edges = np.linspace(college["Expend"].min(), college["Expend"].max(), 4)
count_edges = college["Expend"].quantile([0, 1/3, 2/3, 1])

fig, (ax_width, ax_count) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4), sharey=True,
                                         layout="constrained")
for ax, edges, title in [(ax_width, width_edges, "Equal-width bins: cut()"),
                         (ax_count, count_edges, "Equal-count bins: qcut()")]:
    sns.histplot(data=college, x="Expend", bins=40, ax=ax)
    for edge in edges:
        ax.axvline(edge, color="red", linestyle="--")
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter("${x:,.0f}")
    ax.set(xlabel="Expenditure per student", title=title)

plt.show()








The red lines are the bin edges. np.linspace(low, high, 4) gives four equally spaced numbers, which are the edges cut() used, and quantile([0, 1/3, 2/3, 1]) gives the edges qcut() used. ax.axvline(x) draws a vertical line at x across the panel.
On the left, the equal-width edges are evenly spaced, so almost every college lands left of the first interior line. On the right, the equal-count edges crowd into the dense part of the distribution, so the bins are narrow where colleges are crowded and wide where they are sparse. The 5 highest spenders no longer get a bin of their own; they are simply part of “High”. That is a third way of handling extreme values, alongside the removing and capping in Data Cleaning: an extreme value can only move its bin’s mean, not create an empty bin.
Comparing graduation rates across the tertiles, with the mean for each bar:

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4), layout="constrained")
sns.barplot(data=college, x="expend_level", y="Grad.Rate", ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="Spending per student (tertile)", ylabel="Mean graduation rate (%)")
plt.show()








Graduation rates rise steadily, from 57.3% to 65.9% to 73.0%. As in Data Visualization I, barplot computes the mean of each group for you, the same groupby(...).mean() as above, and the line on each bar is a 95% confidence interval: none of the three intervals overlap. The pattern the scatter plot hinted at is now easy to read, and each bar is backed by 259 colleges.


11.3.4 Bins you choose
Sometimes the edges should come from the question rather than from the data: a budget category, a policy threshold, a grading cutoff. Pass cut() a list of edges instead of a number of bins:

edges = [0, 10_000, 20_000, np.inf]
labels = ["Under $10K", "$10K to $20K", "$20K and over"]

budget_level = pd.cut(college["Expend"], bins=edges, labels=labels, right=False)
budget_level.value_counts(sort=False)

Expend
Under $10K       535
$10K to $20K     214
$20K and over     28
Name: count, dtype: int64


Three details make custom bins behave:

np.inf is infinity, so the last bin has no upper limit and no college can fall outside it. Any value outside the edges you give would become NaN.
right=False closes each interval on the left instead, [left, right), so a college spending exactly $10,000 lands in “$10K to $20K”, which matches how the labels read. Writing 10_000 with an underscore is the same number as 10000, just easier to read.
labels= needs one name per bin: three bins from four edges.

These bins answer a budgeting question — how many colleges spend over $20,000 per student? 28 — at the cost of uneven group sizes, the same trade-off as equal-width bins.
qcut() accepts a list too, but its list holds quantiles rather than values. This splits colleges at the median and the 90th percentile, to set the top 10% of spenders apart:

spending_group = pd.qcut(college["Expend"], [0, 0.5, 0.9, 1],
                         labels=["Bottom half", "50th to 90th percentile", "Top 10%"])
spending_group.value_counts(sort=False)

Expend
Bottom half                389
50th to 90th percentile    310
Top 10%                     78
Name: count, dtype: int64


The list runs from 0 to 1 and the bins hold 50%, 40%, and 10% of the colleges: 389, 310, and 78. Use cut() with a list when the edges are values that mean something, and qcut() with a list when they are shares of the data.


11.3.5 An association, not a recipe
The tertile table invites a recommendation: a college in the low tertile that moved into the high one could expect its graduation rate to rise by about 16 points. The data cannot support that. It shows that colleges which spend more also graduate more students, not that spending more causes higher graduation. High-spending colleges differ in other ways too, and one of them is easy to check:

college.groupby("expend_level")[["Grad.Rate", "Top10perc"]].mean().round(1)








Grad.Rate
Top10perc


expend_level






Low
57.3
17.6


Medium
65.9
24.9


High
73.0
40.1







High-spending colleges admit far more students from the top 10% of their high-school class: 40% against 18%. Students who arrive better prepared are more likely to graduate wherever they enrol, so selectivity alone could produce much of the pattern. Binning makes a pattern easier to see; it does not make it a cause. Describe what you find as an association — “colleges in the highest spending tertile had a mean graduation rate 16 points higher than those in the lowest” — and name what else could explain it.

title: 11  Data Preparation
text:
11.4 Encode categories as numbers
The binned spending levels you just made are categories, and so is Private. Working with them in most analyses requires one more step: turning the categories into numbers.
Why encode categorical variables?

Most statistical and machine-learning methods — correlation, regression, k-nearest neighbors, k-means — do arithmetic on their inputs, so every input must be a number.
Categorical columns often carry some of the most useful information in a dataset, such as whether a college is public or private. Leaving them out because they are text throws that information away.
The way you turn categories into numbers is itself a claim. Codes 0, 1, 2 assert an order and equal steps, so a poor encoding can mislead a model even when the code runs without errors.

Asking pandas how Private relates to graduation rates shows the problem at once:

try:
    college["Private"].corr(college["Grad.Rate"])
except ValueError as error:
    print("ValueError:", error)

ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'Yes'


A correlation is computed from arithmetic on both columns, and "Yes" cannot take part in arithmetic. The try/except lets the notebook show the error and keep running, as in NumPy Fundamentals. How you turn categories into numbers depends on whether they have an order.

11.4.1 Two categories: one 0/1 column
A column with only two values becomes a single column of 0s and 1s. map(), from Pandas Intermediate, replaces each value using a dictionary:

college["private_code"] = college["Private"].map({"No": 0, "Yes": 1})

The counts match the original column, 565 private colleges and 212 public ones, which is the check worth making after any encoding: a value missing from the dictionary would have become NaN. A 0/1 column is easy to read: its mean, college["private_code"].mean(), is the proportion of private colleges.
The correlation that failed a moment ago now works:

print(round(college["private_code"].corr(college["Grad.Rate"]), 2))

0.34


A correlation of 0.34 says private colleges tend to have higher graduation rates. With a 0/1 column the comparison is easy to check directly: private colleges average about 69% and public ones about 56%.


11.4.2 Ordered categories: a code that keeps the order
The spending tertiles have a natural order, so codes 0, 1, and 2 keep a meaning — higher code, higher spending:

level_codes = {"Low": 0, "Medium": 1, "High": 2}
college["expend_code"] = college["expend_level"].map(level_codes)

This is ordinal encoding. It is only safe when the order is real. Coding three majors as Biology = 0, CS = 1, Math = 2 would tell any method that CS sits between the other two and that Math is “twice” CS, which means nothing. Even for ordered categories, codes 0, 1, 2 claim the steps are equal: that “Low” to “Medium” is the same distance as “Medium” to “High”. When that is doubtful, use the next encoding instead.


11.4.3 One indicator column per category
pd.get_dummies() turns a column with k categories into k indicator (or dummy) columns, each 1 where the row belongs to that category and 0 elsewhere. A small list of majors shows the idea:

majors = pd.Series(["Math", "Biology", "CS", "Math", "CS"], name="major")

No order is implied: each major gets its own column, and every row has exactly one 1. dtype=int asks for 0s and 1s instead of True and False. This is called one-hot encoding.
One-hot encoding also suits the spending tertiles, even though they are ordered. Their steps are far from equal: the edge figure showed “Medium” spanning about $2,300, from $7,334 to $9,682, while “High” spans more than $46,000. Codes 0, 1, 2 would treat those two steps as the same size. Indicator columns make no claim about step size at all.
The same function works on a DataFrame column. prefix= names the new columns after their source, and pd.concat(..., axis=1), from Pandas Fundamentals, attaches them beside the original columns:

expend_dummies = pd.get_dummies(college["expend_level"], prefix="expend", dtype=int)

title: 11  Data Preparation
text:
11.5 Rescale numeric columns
Feature scaling is a crucial step in data preparation, especially for machine learning algorithms that are sensitive to the scale of input features. Scaling ensures that numerical features contribute equally to model training and prevents features with larger ranges from dominating those with smaller ranges.
Why scale features?

Many algorithms (e.g., k-nearest neighbors, k-means, principal component analysis, gradient descent-based models) compute distances or rely on feature magnitude.
Features with larger scales can unduly influence the model if not scaled.

A feature is a column a method uses as an input; in this chapter, it is simply a column. The college columns are measured on very different scales:

scale_cols = ["Apps", "Outstate", "Grad.Rate"]

Amherst graduates 100% of its students and Bowdoin 96%, a real difference, yet graduation rate contributes 0.0% of the distance between them. A 4-point gap is invisible next to differences of hundreds of applications and dollars. Any method built on this distance would effectively ignore graduation rates.
Rescaling puts the columns on a common scale so that each one counts according to how unusual its difference is, not how big its units are. It changes the units, never the order of the values within a column.

11.5.1 Min–max scaling
Min–max scaling maps each column onto the range 0 to 1:
\[x_{\text{scaled}} = \frac{x - \min(x)}{\max(x) - \min(x)}\]
This is what MinMaxScaler did before KNN imputation in Data Cleaning. With pandas it is one line, applied to all three columns at once:

minmax = (raw - raw.min()) / (raw.max() - raw.min())
minmax.describe().round(2)

11.5.2 Standardization
Standardization converts each value into a z-score, the same measure the outlier rule in Data Cleaning used: how many standard deviations the value is from its column’s mean.

standardized = (raw - raw.mean()) / raw.std()

Every column now has mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Unlike min–max scaling, the result has no fixed range: the most extreme application count sits 11.65 standard deviations above the mean. A z-score says how unusual a value is, which is often what a comparison across columns needs.
Back to Amherst and Bowdoin, measured in standard deviations:

diff_z = standardized.loc[pair[0]] - standardized.loc[pair[1]]
(diff_z**2 / (diff_z**2).sum()).round(3).rename("share of squared distance")

Grad.Rate    0.372
Name: share of squared distance, dtype: float64


Graduation rate now contributes 37% of the distance. Measured in standard deviations, the three differences are about the same size: 946 applications is 0.24 of a standard deviation of 3,870, the $730 tuition gap is 0.18 of $4,023, and the 4-point gap in graduation rate is 0.23 of 17.1 points. Each column now counts by how unusual its difference is, not by how big its units are.
Plotting the columns side by side before and after shows what changed and what did not:

fig, (ax_raw, ax_z) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4), layout="constrained")

sns.boxplot(data=raw, ax=ax_raw)
ax_raw.set(title="Original units", ylabel="Value")

sns.boxplot(data=standardized, ax=ax_z)
ax_z.set(title="Standardized", ylabel="Standard deviations from the mean")

plt.show()








Passing a whole DataFrame as data= draws one box per column. On the left, graduation rate is invisible next to applications; on the right, all three are comparable. The shapes have not changed: applications are just as right-skewed after standardizing as before. Rescaling is a linear change of units. To reduce skew you need a transformation such as the log in Data Cleaning.






NoteTwo standard deviations



raw.std() divides by \(n - 1\) (pandas’ default, ddof=1). scikit-learn’s StandardScaler divides by \(n\) (ddof=0), like NumPy, so its z-scores are larger by a factor of \(\sqrt{777/776}\): less than 0.1% for 777 rows. Either is fine as long as you use one consistently; NumPy Fundamentals covers ddof.




11.5.3 What not to rescale
Rescale only columns that measure a quantity. Leave these alone:

Indicator and 0/1 columns such as expend_Medium or private_code. A 0/1 column already has a clear meaning — in the category or not — and standardizing it would turn its values into numbers like −1.6 and 0.6 that mean nothing to a reader.
Ordinal codes such as expend_code. The codes are labels for an order, not measurements, so their mean and standard deviation are not meaningful.
Identifiers such as an ID number. They are not quantities at all.










Method
Formula
Result
Use when




Min–max
(x - x.min()) / (x.max() - x.min())
Every column from 0 to 1
You need a fixed range, e.g. before KNN


Standardization
(x - x.mean()) / x.std()
Mean 0, SD 1
You want “how unusual” in common units



Not every method needs rescaling at all. Rescaling matters for methods that combine columns, through distances as in KNN or through weighted sums. Methods that look at one column at a time, such as the decision trees you will meet in later courses, which split the data at a threshold on a single column, give the same result on raw and rescaled data.

Binning.







Goal

Encoding.







Goal
Code




Two categories to 0/1

Ordered categories to codes

One indicator column per category

Drop one as the reference
add drop_first=True


Attach new columns

Rescaling.



Goal
Code




Min–max to [0, 1]
(df - df.min()) / (df.max() - df.min())


Standardize to z-scores
(df - df.mean()) / df.std()


Do not rescale
indicator columns, ordinal codes, identifiers



The rule to remember: check every preparation step — the bin counts, the encoded values, the rescaled ranges — before you analyse the result.

title: 11  Data Preparation
text:
11.9 Before You Move On
The habit to carry forward is checking each preparation step before you trust it. Binning hides detail and can hide a problem with it, which is why the counts come first. Encoding replaces words with numbers that carry claims about order and distance. Rescaling changes units and, if applied to the wrong columns, meaning. Each check is one line, and each catches a mistake that would otherwise travel silently into every result that follows.
The other habit is saying what a prepared comparison does and does not show. A cleaner picture of a pattern is still a picture of an association.
For any dataset you prepare, you should be able to answer five questions:

Why did you bin this column, and why these edges?
How many rows fell into each bin?
Does the pattern across bins have another explanation you can check?
Which encoding did each categorical column get, and does it imply an order that is not there?
Which columns did you rescale, and which did you deliberately leave alone?

Continue to Data Grouping and Aggregation, where the groupby() you have been using for one mean at a time becomes a full tool for summarizing data by group.
References: pd.cut, pd.qcut, Series.map, pd.get_dummies, pd.concat, DataFrame.groupby, and scikit-learn StandardScaler.

title: 12  Data Grouping and Aggregation
text:
12.1 Set Up Your Chapter Files
The last two chapters used groupby() in its simplest form: one grouping column, one statistic, such as a continent’s mean GDP to fill a gap in Data Cleaning or a spending tertile’s mean graduation rate in Data Preparation. That one line is an instance of a general pattern, and most summaries in data analysis follow it: split the rows into groups, compute something within each group, and combine the results into a table.
This chapter makes that pattern a full tool. It covers counting by category, computing several statistics at once with readable names, grouping by more than one column, and the three things you can do with groups besides summarizing them: give every row a group-level value, keep or drop whole groups, and take a few rows from each. Along the way it asks a question every grouped summary raises: what exactly is being averaged?
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:
Complete the practice activity after the worked examples.
Download the Data Grouping and Aggregation practice kit. Extract stat303-data-aggregation inside the chapters folder of your stat303-1 course folder, open stat303-1 in VS Code, and select the course environment. The terminal opens in stat303-1, so move it into the kit with cd chapters and then cd stat303-data-aggregation before you render the activity.
Run data_aggregation_examples.ipynb for the lesson and complete activity12.ipynb for your own activity report, with stat303-data-aggregation as the notebook working folder. The data is read with the relative path "data/gdp_lifeExpectancy.csv", so the notebooks find it only when that folder is the working folder.

title: 12  Data Grouping and Aggregation
text:
12.4 Split, apply, combine
Counting is one summary per group. Most questions need others — a mean, a median, a total — and the tool that computes any of them by group is groupby().
Why group and aggregate?

Summarize a large table. Thousands of rows become one row per group that a reader can take in: total sales by region instead of every transaction.
Compare categories. Patterns become visible when groups sit side by side: outcomes by treatment group, graduation rates by type of college, life expectancy by continent.
Follow groups over time. Grouping by a time period — month, quarter, year — turns a stream of records into a trend you can plot.
Reduce complexity. A summary at the right level answers the question without the noise of every individual row.

Every one of these works the same way. groupby() follows three steps, a pattern known as split–apply–combine:

Split the rows into groups, one per distinct value of the grouping column.
Apply a computation to each group separately.
Combine the results into one Series or DataFrame, labelled by group.




Split–apply–combine: six rows are split by ID into three groups, each group is summed, and the three sums are combined into one table.


The diagram’s six rows, as a DataFrame, give exactly its result:

toy = pd.DataFrame({"ID": ["X", "Y", "Z", "X", "Y", "Z"],
                    "Values": [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]})
toy.groupby("ID")["Values"].sum()

ID
X    50
Y    70
Z    90
Name: Values, dtype: int64


Split puts rows with the same ID together (X holds 10 and 40), apply sums each group, and combine stacks the three sums into one Series labelled by ID: X = 50, Y = 70, Z = 90. The same three steps run on the GDP data, only with more rows.

title: 12  Data Grouping and Aggregation
text:
12.7 What a group mean averages
Each value in that plot is a mean over countries: Mongolia and China count equally toward Asia’s figure. That answers the question “what was life expectancy in a typical Asian country?” It does not answer “how long did a typical person in Asia live?”, because China and India hold most of Asia’s people.
The second question needs a weighted mean, in which each country counts in proportion to its population:
\[\text{weighted mean} = \frac{\sum (\text{pop} \times \text{lifeExp})}{\sum \text{pop}}\]
groupby() can compute both sums at once. Make a column of the products, sum it and pop by group, and divide:

gdp["pop_x_life"] = gdp["pop"] * gdp["lifeExp"]
sums = gdp.groupby(["continent", "year"])[["pop_x_life", "pop"]].sum()
weighted_life = sums["pop_x_life"] / sums["pop"]

asia = pd.DataFrame({
    "per country (unweighted)": life_by_year.loc["Asia"],
    "per person (weighted by population)": weighted_life.loc["Asia"],
}).round(1)
asia.loc[[1952, 1982, 2007]]

per person (weighted by population)


year

In 1952 the typical Asian country had a life expectancy of 46.3 years, but the typical Asian person only 42.9, because the most populous countries had some of the lowest values. Dividing two group sums keeps everything aligned by the shared continent–year index, so each weighted mean uses its own group’s numbers.
Plotting both versions over every year shows something the three rows hide. asia.plot(), the pandas plotting from Data Visualization I, draws one line per column against the index:

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5), layout="constrained")
asia.plot(ax=ax, marker="o")
ax.set(xlabel="Year", ylabel="Life expectancy in Asia (years)",
       title="Per person, Asia's life expectancy fell in 1962; per country, it rose")
plt.show()








Between 1957 and 1962 the per-country line keeps rising, but the per-person line falls, from 47.3 to 46.6 years, and the gap between them jumps to 5 years. The cause is one country. China’s life expectancy dropped from 50.5 years in 1957 to 44.5 in 1962, the years of the famine of 1959–1961, and China held 39% of Asia’s people. In a per-country mean China is one country in 33, so the drop barely registers; weighted by population, it dominates.
Neither mean is wrong; they answer different questions. When you report a group mean, say which one it is — per country, per person, per college — because the reader cannot tell from the number.

title: 12  Data Grouping and Aggregation
section: 12.8 Give every row a group value: transform()
text:
12.8 Give every row a group value: transform()
Summaries return one row per group. Sometimes you want the group value on every row instead, to compare each row with its own group. Data Cleaning used transform("mean") to fill a missing GDP with its continent’s mean; the same tool answers “how does each country compare with its continent in the same year?”:

continent_year_mean = gdp.groupby(["continent", "year"])["gdpPercap"].transform("mean")
gdp["gdp_vs_continent"] = gdp["gdpPercap"] / continent_year_mean

gdp.loc[gdp["year"] == 2007,
        ["country", "continent", "gdpPercap", "gdp_vs_continent"]].sort_values(

title: 12  Data Grouping and Aggregation
section: 12.9 Keep or drop whole groups: filter()
text:
12.9 Keep or drop whole groups: filter()
filter() tests each group against a rule and keeps all the rows of the groups that pass. The rule is a function that receives one group as a DataFrame and returns True or False. Which countries gained more than 30 years of life expectancy between 1952 and 2007?

big_gainers = gdp.groupby("country").filter(
    lambda g: g["lifeExp"].max() - g["lifeExp"].min() > 30
)
print(big_gainers["country"].nunique(), "countries")
big_gainers["country"].unique()

9 countries


<StringArray>
[         'Indonesia',        'Korea, Rep.',              'Libya',
          'Nicaragua',               'Oman',       'Saudi Arabia',
            'Vietnam', 'West Bank and Gaza',        'Yemen, Rep.']
Length: 9, dtype: str


Every row of those 9 countries is kept, all 12 years each, so the result can be plotted or summarized like the full data. A Boolean mask on rows, by contrast, tests each row on its own:

over_70 = gdp[gdp["lifeExp"] > 70]
print(len(over_70), "rows from", over_70["country"].nunique(), "countries")

493 rows from 84 countries


The mask keeps every country-year above 70, so most of those 84 countries appear only for their later years. Use a mask for a rule about a row, and filter() for a rule about a group as a whole.

12.13 Extended Practice
These longer exercises are additional practice, not requirements for the Canvas quiz. Work in a separate notebook beside your activity and load the data the way the chapter does. Include your code, outputs, and explanations.

12.13.1 The World Over Time, Two Ways
Compute world life expectancy for every year twice, per country and per person, and plot both lines on one figure. When are the two furthest apart, and which countries drive the gap? Repeat for GDP per capita.


12.13.2 Correlation Within Each Continent
For each continent, compute the correlation between lifeExp and gdpPercap over all years. Unlike agg(), which hands its function one column of each group, apply() hands it the whole group as a DataFrame, so the function can use two columns at once: gdp.groupby("continent")[["lifeExp", "gdpPercap"]].apply(lambda g: g["lifeExp"].corr(g["gdpPercap"])). Then repeat with np.log(gdpPercap). Which continents change most, and why might a log make the relationship more linear?


12.13.3 Biggest Gains and Losses
For each country, compute the change in life expectancy from each survey year to the next. Which country had the largest single five-year drop, and when? The hint is diff(), which subtracts each value from the one after it: gdp.sort_values(["country", "year"]).groupby("country")["lifeExp"].diff(). Grouping by country means one country’s last year is never compared with the next country’s first.


12.13.4 A Fair Sample
Draw a stratified sample of 10 countries per continent (all 12 years of each), rather than 10 rows. Hint: sample from the 2007 rows to choose the countries, then keep every row for those countries with isin(). Compare the mean life expectancy of your sample with the full data’s.

title: 12  Data Grouping and Aggregation
text:
12.14 Before You Move On
The habit to carry forward is knowing what a group summary counts. A count of rows is not a count of units; a mean over countries is not a mean over people; a continent with two countries is not comparable, on equal terms, with a continent of fifty. None of these produces an error, and every one changes what a summary table says.
The other habit is choosing the operation by the shape of the result you need: one row per group to summarize, every row with a group value to compare, whole groups to keep or drop, or a few rows from each group to sample.
For any grouped summary you make or read, you should be able to answer five questions:

What are the groups, and how many rows and distinct units does each contain?
Which statistic summarizes each group, and why that one?
Does each row count equally, and should it?
Is the data balanced across groups and over time?
Did you need one row per group, or a group value on every row?

Continue to Data Reshaping, where grouped results like these are rearranged between long and wide tables.
References: pandas: group by (split-apply-combine), DataFrame.groupby, DataFrameGroupBy.agg, DataFrameGroupBy.transform, DataFrameGroupBy.filter, DataFrameGroupBy.sample, pd.crosstab, and DataFrame.reset_index.

text:
13.1 Set Up Your Chapter Files
Data Grouping and Aggregation ended with a grouped result indexed by continent and year, and a promise: turning it into a table with one column per year is reshaping. The same information can be laid out with many rows and few columns, or few rows and many columns, and different tasks need different layouts. A plot that colours lines by group wants one layout; a comparison of two years side by side wants the other.
This chapter is about moving data between those layouts without changing a single value. It covers turning a long table wide, turning a wide table long, and the checks that confirm nothing was lost, duplicated, or quietly averaged along the way.

title: 13  Data Reshaping
text:
13.2 What reshaping is
Reshaping changes the structure of a table without changing the information in it. Think of rearranging the furniture in a room: every piece is still there, but the layout suits a different purpose. The same values can be arranged in two basic layouts:

Long format stacks the values into few columns and many rows. Each row is one observation: one country in one year, with its life expectancy.
Wide format spreads the values across many columns and few rows. Each row is one unit, such as a country, with one column per year.

A small example with three countries and three years shows both. The data starts long:

toy_long = pd.DataFrame({
    "country": ["USA", "USA", "USA", "Canada", "Canada", "Canada", "Mexico", "Mexico", "Mexico"],
    "year": [2000, 2005, 2010] * 3,
    "lifeExp": [76.8, 77.5, 78.5, 79.2, 80.1, 81.0, 74.1, 75.2, 76.5],
})

NoteTidy data



You will often see long format described as tidy data: each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each value is a cell. In the long table, country, year, and lifeExp are each one column, and each row is one observation. In the wide table, the single variable “year” is spread across three column headers. Tidy data is what groupby(), seaborn, and most statistical tools expect, which is why data is so often melted before it is analysed.


Why reshaping matters.

Different tools need different layouts. Seaborn’s hue= and col=, from the visualization chapters, expect long data: one column holding the group. A comparison of 1957 with 2007 is one subtraction in wide data, with each year its own column.
Some calculations are easy in one layout and awkward in the other. Change over time per country is a column difference when wide; a mean per year is a groupby() when long.
Combining datasets needs matching layouts. Two tables can only be joined row by row once each row means the same thing in both, the subject of the next chapter.

pivot() turns the values of one column into column headers. 13.4.2 Why wide: two years side by side
With one row per country and one column per year, comparing any two years is easy. A scatter plot of 1957 against 2007 shows every country’s 50-year change at once. reset_index() turns the two index levels back into columns for seaborn:

plot_data = country_wide.reset_index()

ax.set(xlabel="Life expectancy in 1957 (years)", ylabel="Life expectancy in 2007 (years)",
       title="Almost every country gained; four did not")
ax.legend(loc="lower right")
plt.show()








Points above the dashed line gained life expectancy over 50 years; points below it lost. Selecting the countries below the line is one comparison of two columns:

This is the region the HIV/AIDS epidemic of the 1990s and 2000s hit hardest, and it is why Africa’s average stalled in the last chapter’s trend plot. In long format, finding these four would take a filter, a groupby(), and a comparison across rows; in wide format it is one line.
A wide table is also exactly what a heatmap draws, as in Data Visualization I. Europe’s 30 countries, each a row:

europe_wide = country_wide.loc["Europe"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 8), layout="constrained")

The lightest rows at the start — Turkey, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Albania — show where Europe’s lowest life expectancies were in 1952.






TipTurning a wide table on its side



A wide table with many columns can be easier to read turned on its side. .T, the transpose from NumPy Fundamentals, swaps rows and columns: country_wide.T has one row per year and one column per country. Unlike pivot() and melt(), it does not change which values sit together; it only turns the table.




13.4.3 Summarizing while reshaping: pivot_table()
A continent-by-year table is a different request. Each continent-year cell would have to hold every country of that continent in that year — 52 for Africa — and pivot() will not choose among them:

try:
    gdp.pivot(index="continent", columns="year", values="lifeExp")
except ValueError as error:
    print("ValueError:", error)

ValueError: Index contains duplicate entries, cannot reshape


To fill such a cell, the rows that land in it must be summarized into one number, and only you know which summary you want. pivot_table() takes the same three arguments as pivot(), plus aggfunc=, the function that combines the rows in each cell. Here it is the mean life expectancy of each continent’s countries:

                               aggfunc="mean", margins=True)
print("All row, 2007:", round(life_margins.loc["All", 2007], 1))
print("mean of the five continent means, 2007:", round(life_pivot[2007].mean(), 1))

All row, 2007: 67.0

The All row is the mean over all 142 countries, 67.0 years in 2007, not the mean of the five continent means, 71.5. Africa’s 52 countries count 26 times as much as Oceania’s two. It is the same question as in the last chapter — what does this mean average? — and the margin answers it differently from what a reader of the table might assume.


13.4.4 The same table from a grouped result: unstack()
The last chapter built this table in two steps. Grouping by two columns gives a Series with a two-level index: continent on the outer level and year on the inner. unstack() moves the inner level up into the column headers, so each continent becomes one row and each year one column:

life_by_year = gdp.groupby(["continent", "year"])["lifeExp"].mean()
life_wide = life_by_year.unstack()
print(life_wide.equals(life_pivot))

True


equals() confirms the two tables are identical: pivot_table() does the grouping and the unstacking in one call. Use unstack() when you already have a grouped result. Either way, with years as columns, change over time is one subtraction:

(life_wide[2007] - life_wide[1952]).round(1).sort_values()

Africa gained 15.7 years over the period and Asia 24.4.


13.4.5 Rearrange or summarize? What a duplicate does
The choice between pivot() and pivot_table() matters most when the data has a mistake. Suppose the three-country table had Canada’s 2005 value entered twice, with a typo in the second entry. pd.concat(), from Pandas Fundamentals, adds the extra row; ignore_index=True numbers the rows afresh. pivot() stops at the duplicate:

toy_dup = pd.concat([toy_long,
                     pd.DataFrame({"country": ["Canada"], "year": [2005], "lifeExp": [80.5]})],
                    ignore_index=True)

try:
    toy_dup.pivot(index="country", columns="year", values="lifeExp")
except ValueError as error:
    print("ValueError:", error)

ValueError: Index contains duplicate entries, cannot reshape


pivot_table() does not stop. It does what it was told, and averages the two rows:

toy_dup.pivot_table(index="country", columns="year", values="lifeExp", aggfunc="mean")

When you mean to summarize, use pivot_table(), name the summary in aggfunc=, and check the counts if any cell should have held one row. A duplicate is the kind of row duplicated(subset=["country", "year"]) from Data Cleaning finds before you reshape.

13.5 Wide to long

13.5.1 melt()
Data often arrives wide because that is how people record and publish it: a spreadsheet with one row per student and one column per quiz, or a public data download — from the World Bank or the Census Bureau, say — with one row per country or state and one column per year. With such data, melt() is usually the first step. melt() turns those columns into rows, the inverse of pivoting. A small gradebook shows the idea:

grades = pd.DataFrame({
    "student": ["Ana", "Ben", "Chen", "Dee"],
    "quiz1": [8, 6, 9, 7],
    "quiz2": [9, 7, 9, 6],
    "quiz3": [7, 8, 10, 8],
})

Four students × three quizzes = 12 rows. The three arguments say what to keep and what to call the new columns:








Argument
Meaning
Here

Columns that identify a row and stay as they are
student


var_name=

score



Every column not listed in id_vars is melted; value_vars= limits the melt to some of them. In long form, the questions a gradebook raises become one familiar line each — the mean score on each quiz is a groupby():

grades_long.groupby("quiz")["score"].mean()

quiz
quiz1    7.50
quiz2    7.75
quiz3    8.25
Name: score, dtype: float64


Long format is also what seaborn’s hue= needs, here to draw one line per student:

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4), layout="constrained")
sns.lineplot(data=grades_long, x="quiz", y="score", hue="student", marker="o", ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="Score (out of 10)")
plt.show()










13.5.2 Melting back, and checking the result
The country-by-year table melts back into the original long layout. reset_index() first turns continent and country into ordinary columns, so they can be id_vars:

life_long = country_wide.reset_index().melt(id_vars=["continent", "country"],
                                           var_name="year", value_name="lifeExp")
print(life_long.shape)
print(life_long.dtypes)

(1704, 4)
continent        str
country          str
year          object
lifeExp      float64
dtype: object


142 countries × 12 years = 1,704 rows, matching the original data. But year came back as object, not as integers: the year labels passed through column headers, where they were stored alongside the text headers continent and country. A reshape can change a column’s type without any warning, so check dtypes afterwards and restore it:

life_long["year"] = life_long["year"].astype(int)

original = gdp.sort_values(["country", "year"]).reset_index(drop=True)
restored = life_long.sort_values(["country", "year"]).reset_index(drop=True)
print("same years:", (original["year"] == restored["year"]).all())
print("same values:", np.allclose(original["lifeExp"], restored["lifeExp"]))

same years: True
same values: True


Sorted the same way, the melted table matches the original row for row: long to wide and back again lost nothing. This round-trip check — reshape, reshape back, compare — is the surest way to confirm a reshape did only what you meant.


13.5.3 stack()
stack() is the counterpart of unstack(): it moves the column headers down into the inner level of the row index, turning the continent-by-year table back into a Series:

life_stacked = life_wide.stack()
print(life_stacked.shape)
life_stacked.head()

(60,)


continent  year
Africa     1952    39.135500
           1957    41.266346
           1962    43.319442
           1967    45.334538
           1972    47.450942
dtype: float64


60 values again, indexed by continent and year: exactly the grouped result the section started from. Use stack() and unstack() when the data already has a two-level index, as grouped results do, and melt(), pivot(), and pivot_table() when it has ordinary columns.

title: 13  Data Reshaping
text:
13.9 Before You Move On
The habit to carry forward is checking a reshape. Every tool in this chapter can return a perfectly shaped table that is wrong: pivot_table() averages a duplicate without saying so, margins=True averages over rows rather than groups, and melt() can bring numbers back as text. Count the rows, look at what each cell combined, and check the types — or reshape back and compare.
Choose pivot() when each cell should hold one value, so a duplicate stops it, and pivot_table() with a named aggfunc= when you mean to summarize.
The other habit is choosing the layout by the task. Long data suits groupby(), seaborn, and models; wide data suits comparisons between columns and tables for a reader.
For any reshape you make, you should be able to answer five questions:

Is the starting table long or wide, and what is one row?
What will one row and one column be after the reshape?
Did any cell combine more than one value, and if so, how?
Does the row count after the reshape match what you expected?
Did any column change type?

Continue to Combining Datasets, where tables in matching layouts are joined together.
References: pandas: reshaping and pivot tables, DataFrame.pivot, DataFrame.pivot_table, DataFrame.melt, DataFrame.stack, DataFrame.unstack, and DataFrame.T.

title: 14  Combining Datasets
text:
14.1 Set Up Your Chapter Files
Data Reshaping ended with a condition: two tables can be joined row by row only once each row means the same thing in both. This chapter does the joining. Real analyses rarely start from a single table. The information you need is split across files — one per region or per year, one holding measurements and another holding descriptions — and the first job is often to put it back together.
There are two basic ways to combine tables. When they hold the same kind of rows, you stack them. When they hold different information about the same things, you match their rows on a shared key. Matching is where the surprises live: rows that find no partner, keys that appear twice, names spelled differently in two sources. So, as in the last two chapters, the habit to build is checking the result before you trust it.
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:
Complete the practice activity after the worked examples.
Download the Combining Datasets practice kit. Extract stat303-combining-datasets inside the chapters folder of your stat303-1 course folder, open stat303-1 in VS Code, and select the course environment. The terminal opens in stat303-1, so move it into the kit with cd chapters and then cd stat303-combining-datasets before you render the activity.
Run combining_datasets_examples.ipynb for the lesson and complete activity14.ipynb for your own activity report, with stat303-combining-datasets as the notebook working folder. Every file is read with a relative path such as "data/gdp_lifeExpec_Asia.csv", so the notebooks find their data only when that folder is the working folder.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

title: 14  Combining Datasets
text:
14.2 Why combine datasets
Why combine?

Information is distributed. Customer details live in one table and purchases in another; product descriptions are separate from sales; a survey’s answers are split across several files.
Data comes from several sources. Internal records meet external data — a company’s sales with public economic indicators, or a course’s grades with its attendance log.
Data is split for storage. One file per month, per region, or per year is common, and an analysis across all of them needs them in one table.
An analysis needs more columns. Adding a population, a region, or a category from a second table makes new comparisons possible.

Two operations cover nearly every case:









Operation
Tool
The tables share
Result




Stack
pd.concat()
The same columns, different rows
More rows


Match
df.merge()
A key column, different information
More columns, rows paired by key

title: 14  Combining Datasets
text:
14.3 Stack rows: pd.concat()
The Gapminder data from the last two chapters arrives here in pieces: one file per continent, each with the same five columns. Combining them is stacking, and pd.concat(), which you met adding a row in Data Reshaping, does it for a whole list of tables.
None of the files has a continent column — the continent is in the file name. Adding it as each file is read keeps that information once the pieces are stacked. A for loop reads each file, adds the column, and collects the pieces in a list:

pieces = []
for continent in ["Africa", "Americas", "Asia", "Europe", "Oceania"]:
    piece = pd.read_csv(f"data/gdp_lifeExpec_{continent}.csv")
    piece["continent"] = continent
    print(continent, piece.shape)
    pieces.append(piece)

gapminder = pd.concat(pieces, ignore_index=True)
print("stacked:", gapminder.shape)

concat() lines up columns by name. A column that some pieces lack is filled with NaN in the rows from those pieces. Suppose the Africa file had spelled one column differently:

renamed = pieces[0].rename(columns={"lifeExp": "life_expectancy"})   # the Africa piece

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5), layout="constrained")

title: 14  Combining Datasets
section: 14.4 Match rows on a key: merge()
text:
14.4 Match rows on a key: merge()
Stacking needs tables with the same columns. Matching needs something different: a key, a column whose values identify the same thing in both tables. Two small tables about members of the Fellowship from The Lord of the Rings show how it works. One lists skills, the other ages, and both identify members by FellowshipID:

skills = pd.DataFrame({
    "FellowshipID": [1001, 1002, 1003, 1004],
    "FirstName": ["Frodo", "Samwise", "Gandalf", "Pippin"],
    "Skills": ["Hiding", "Gardening", "Spells", "Fireworks"],
})
ages = pd.DataFrame({
    "FellowshipID": [1001, 1002, 1006, 1007, 1008],
    "FirstName": ["Frodo", "Samwise", "Legolas", "Elrond", "Boromir"],
    "Age": [50, 39, 2931, 6520, 51],
})
print(skills, "\n")
print(ages)

0          1001     Frodo     Hiding
1          1002   Samwise  Gardening
2          1003   Gandalf     Spells
3          1004    Pippin  Fireworks

0          1001     Frodo    50
1          1002   Samwise    39
2          1006   Legolas  2931
3          1007    Elrond  6520
4          1008   Boromir    51


Frodo and Samwise appear in both tables; Gandalf and Pippin only in skills; Legolas, Elrond, and Boromir only in ages. merge() pairs rows whose key values are equal:

Both tables have a FirstName column that is not part of the key, so pandas keeps both and adds suffixes: _x from the left table, _y from the right. Here the two columns agree, because a name belongs to its ID.

14.4.1 Several key columns

how=
Use when
Examples




"inner"
The analysis needs both pieces of information for every row
Relating vaccination rates to infection rates: only countries with both can contribute. An A/B test: only users with both a group assignment and an outcome count.


"left"
The left table is your primary data and every row must stay
All customers with their purchases: a customer with no purchases spent $0. All employees with their reviews: an employee not yet reviewed is “pending”, not missing.


"outer"
Nothing may be lost from either table
Mid- and end-of-semester surveys: keep every student who answered either one. Auditing expected against actual records: find what is missing on each side.


"right"
The right table is primary

title: 14  Combining Datasets
text:
14.5 Check a merge
A merge can return a table of the right shape that is quietly wrong. Three checks catch most problems: the row count, the uniqueness of the keys, and the missing values that unmatched keys leave behind.

14.5.1 The row count, and keys that repeat
Suppose life expectancy and GDP arrived in two separate tables, both keyed by country and year:

life = gapminder[["country", "year", "lifeExp"]]
money = gapminder[["country", "year", "gdpPercap"]]

both_keys = life.merge(money, on=["country", "year"])
print(life.shape, money.shape, "->", both_keys.shape)

(1704, 3) (1704, 3) -> (1704, 4)


1,704 rows in, 1,704 rows out: every country-year found exactly one partner. Now the same merge with an incomplete key, country alone:

country_only = life.merge(money, on="country")
print(country_only.shape)

20,448 rows: twelve times too many, and no error. Each country has 12 rows in each table, so every row in life pairs with all 12 rows of the same country in money, and 12 × 12 = 144 rows per country × 142 countries = 20,448. The year_x and year_y columns are the giveaway: a 1952 life expectancy sits beside a 2007 GDP. A key must identify one row; country alone does not.
validate= tells merge() what you expect and raises an error when the keys disagree. "one_to_one" means each key appears at most once in each table; "many_to_one" means the right table’s keys are unique, as for a lookup table. A try/except block shows the error and lets the notebook keep running:

try:
    life.merge(money, on="country", validate="one_to_one")
except pd.errors.MergeError as error:
    print("MergeError:", str(error).splitlines()[0])

MergeError: Merge keys are not unique in either left or right dataset; not a one-to-one merge.


The same check passes for the correct key, on=["country", "year"]. Add validate= whenever you know how the tables should relate; it turns a silent row explosion into an error you cannot miss. Before merging, df.duplicated(subset=key).sum(), from Data Cleaning, counts repeated keys in each table.


14.5.2 Many rows to one: a lookup table
The most common merge in practice attaches a small lookup table to many rows: a region for each state, a price for each product code, a group summary for each member. Each row of the large table matches exactly one row of the lookup table, while each lookup row matches many — the "many_to_one" relationship.
A summary from Data Grouping and Aggregation makes a lookup table: mean life expectancy for each continent and year, 60 rows. rename() gives its value column a distinct name before the merge:

continent_mean = (gapminder.groupby(["continent", "year"])["lifeExp"].mean()
                  .reset_index()
                  .rename(columns={"lifeExp": "continent_lifeExp"}))

with_mean = gapminder.merge(continent_mean, on=["continent", "year"],
                            how="left", validate="many_to_one")
print(continent_mean.shape, "->", with_mean.shape)

(60, 3) -> (1704, 7)


validate="many_to_one" passes because each continent-year appears once in the lookup table, and the row count is still 1,704: every country row gained one value and none was duplicated. That is the check for any lookup merge — the row count must not change.
Each country can now be compared with its continent in the same year:

with_mean["gap"] = with_mean["lifeExp"] - with_mean["continent_lifeExp"]

A left or outer merge fills the columns of unmatched rows with NaN. Unlike the gaps in Data Cleaning, these mean something specific: this key was not found in the other table. The right handling depends on what absence means.

Gandalf’s and Pippin’s ages are NaN because the ages table has no row for them, not because their age is zero. Three choices, from Data Cleaning:

Keep the NaN when absence is informative and should be reported, as here: the ages table is incomplete.
Fill when absence has a known meaning: a customer with no purchase rows spent $0, so fillna(0) is correct for spend, though it would be wrong for age.
Drop with dropna(subset=[...]) when an analysis needs both values — which is the same as having used an inner join.

You will also meet df.join(other), which matches rows on the index rather than on a column, and pd.concat([a, b], axis=1), which places tables side by side by index. Both do work merge() can do once the key is an ordinary column, which is how this book writes it: merge() names the key, so the match is visible in the code.

title: 14  Combining Datasets
text:
14.9 Before You Move On
The habit to carry forward is checking every combination. A stack should have exactly the rows of its pieces. A merge should have the rows you predicted from its keys and its how=, and indicator=True and validate= turn the ways it can go wrong — unmatched keys, keys that repeat — into numbers and errors you can see. None of these mistakes raises an error on its own; a merged table looks complete whether or not it is right.
The other habit is asking what an absence means. A NaN from an unmatched key says the other table had no row, which is different from a value of zero and different from a measurement that was never taken.
For any combination you make, you should be able to answer five questions:

Are you stacking tables with the same columns, or matching tables on a key?
What is the key, and does it identify exactly one row in each table?
Which how= did you choose, and how many rows did you expect?
How many rows matched, and why did the others not?
What do the missing values from unmatched keys mean, and what did you do with them?

This chapter completes the path the book has followed: reading data, cleaning it, preparing it, summarizing it by group, reshaping it, and now combining it. The assignments in the appendices bring these steps together on larger datasets.
References: pandas: merge, join, concatenate and compare, pd.concat, DataFrame.merge, DataFrame.join, and pandas.errors.MergeError.

section: 1. Build and Organize the Course Folder (20 points)
text:
1. Build and Organize the Course Folder (20 points)
Do these steps in order, using Finder on macOS or File Explorer on Windows to create, delete, and move folders. Close VS Code first, so that nothing is still using the Chapter 2 environment while you change its folder.

Choose a location. Pick a place that cloud storage does not sync, such as your home folder. Avoid the iCloud-synced Desktop and Documents folders on macOS and OneDrive-synced folders on Windows: sync tools can upload, offload, or lock the thousands of small files inside .venv, and that breaks the environment.
Create the folders. Create a folder named stat303-1, and inside it create two folders named chapters and assignments. Use these exact lowercase names, with no spaces.
Retire the Chapter 2 environment. Inside your stat303-setup folder, delete the .venv folder. Keep everything else in stat303-setup, including your activity notebooks, HTML files, data, and requirements.txt.
Move the Chapter 2 folder. Move stat303-setup into stat303-1/chapters/.
Place the assignment kit. Extract the Assignment B ZIP and move the extracted assignment-b folder into stat303-1/assignments/. Check that you did not create a nested assignment-b/assignment-b/ folder.
File Assignment A. Inside assignments, create a folder named assignment-a and move your completed Assignment A notebook and its rendered HTML into it. Assignment A has no data, but it still gets its own folder, so that every assignment follows the same rule and its notebook and rendered output stay together.
Open the course folder. In VS Code, choose File → Open Folder and open stat303-1 itself, not assignments or assignment-b. From now on, this is the folder you open for every chapter and assignment.


1.1 Folder evidence (8 points)
Add your name to the notebook. Open a terminal in VS Code; it starts in stat303-1, the folder you opened. Show the current directory, then list the contents of stat303-1, chapters, and assignments without leaving stat303-1. To list a folder without entering it, put its name after the listing command: ls chapters on macOS, Get-ChildItem chapters in PowerShell, or dir chapters in Command Prompt. Copy the commands and output into your answer. State where you placed stat303-1 and why that location is not synced by cloud storage.
The root listing does not need .venv, README.md, or requirements.txt yet; you create them in later questions.
Credit: three listings showing the required structure, 5 points; location and reason, 2 points; name, 1 point.


1.2 Write a folder guide (6 points)
In VS Code’s Explorer, create a file named README.md directly inside stat303-1, next to chapters and assignments. Write a short guide, in your own words, that a classmate could follow to use the folder. It must say:

which folder to open in VS Code;
where the course environment and its requirements.txt live, and that .venv is never moved or copied;
where a new chapter practice kit goes;
where a new assignment goes, including one that has no data;
that each kit keeps its notebooks beside its own data/ folder when it has one.

Paste the text of your finished README.md into your answer inside a ```text block, so that it displays exactly as written.
Credit: five required points, 1 point each; clear, complete sentences, 1 point.


1.3 Explain the design (6 points)
Answer in your own words:

Why does the course use one .venv at the root of stat303-1, instead of a separate environment inside each chapter kit?
The Python venv documentation says that virtual environments are not movable or copyable, because an environment records the absolute location where it was created. Use this to explain why you deleted the Chapter 2 .venv instead of moving it along with stat303-setup. How will your Chapter 2 notebooks get a working environment now?
Why does each kit keep its own data/ folder, instead of all kits sharing one data folder at the root of stat303-1? Consider the relative path Path("data") / "station_readings.csv" and the folder each notebook starts in.

Credit: three explanations, 2 points each.

text:
1. Air Quality Sensors (30 points)
An application of broadcasting.
Air quality sensors measure the amount of contaminants in air. This question finds locations for 50 air quality sensors in Colorado so that they are as far from each other as possible. The method below is a greedy algorithm that finds an approximate maximin design.
The file data/colorado_coordinate_grid.txt holds the coordinate-pairs (latitude and longitude) of potential sensor locations. A coordinate-pair means a latitude-longitude pair, and “air quality sensor” is shortened to “sensor” below. Measure every distance as the Euclidean distance between coordinate-pairs.
The starter notebook supplies this function, which draws the sensors in air_sensor_coordinates on a map of Colorado:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def sensor_viz():
    """Draw the sensors in air_sensor_coordinates on the map of Colorado."""
    img = plt.imread("data/colorado.jpg")
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.5, 7.7))
    ax.imshow(img, extent=[-109, -102, 37, 41])
    ax.scatter(-air_sensor_coordinates[:, 1], air_sensor_coordinates[:, 0], color="blue")
    ax.set(xlim=(-109.05, -101.95), ylim=(36.95, 41.05),
           xlabel="Longitude", ylabel="Latitude")
    plt.show()

1.1 Read the grid (2 points)
Read the file with NumPy, skipping its header row. How many coordinate-pairs are there?
Hint: np.genfromtxt() with delimiter=",", as in NumPy Fundamentals. The file’s first line holds the column names, Latitude,Longitude, so also pass skip_header=1, which skips that line; otherwise it is read as a row of nan values.


1.2 First sensor (2 points)
The first sensor goes at the grid point closest to Denver, whose coordinate-pair is 39.7392° N, 104.9903° W. The file omits the ° N and ° W, so Denver is [39.7392, 104.9903] in its units. Find the coordinate-pair of the first sensor.
Hint: Broadcasting. grid - denver subtracts Denver’s coordinate-pair from every row at once, ** 2 squares every entry, and np.sqrt() takes the square root element-wise, the way np.round() did in NumPy Fundamentals. Sum the squared differences across each row before taking the square root.


1.3 Second sensor (4 points)
The second sensor goes at the grid point farthest from the first sensor. Find its coordinate-pair.
Hint: Broadcasting.


1.4 The first two sensors (4 points)
Stack the coordinate-pairs of the first and second sensors vertically into a 2 × 2 NumPy array named air_sensor_coordinates. Then run the supplied sensor_viz() to check your work: the two sensors appear as blue dots on the map.


1.5 Third sensor (12 points)
The third sensor goes at the grid point that is farthest from the sensors already placed. Proceed as follows:

For each coordinate-pair in the grid, find its minimum distance from the two sensors already placed. For example, a point 5 units from the first sensor and 10 units from the second has a minimum distance of \(\min(5, 10) = 5\).
Select the coordinate-pair whose minimum distance is the largest.
Stack it vertically onto air_sensor_coordinates, and call sensor_viz() to check that three sensors appear.

Hint: Write a function that takes one coordinate-pair and returns its minimum distance from all the rows of air_sensor_coordinates. Then apply it to every row of the grid with np.apply_along_axis(function, 1, grid), which calls the function once per row (axis 1) and collects the results in an array.


1.6 All 50 sensors (6 points)
Generalize Question 1.5 to place 47 more sensors. With \(i\) sensors placed, find each grid point’s minimum distance from those \(i\) sensors, \(\min(d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_i)\), and place sensor \(i + 1\) at the grid point where that minimum is largest. Repeat until there are 50 sensors. This is one of the two questions where a loop is allowed.
Call sensor_viz() at the end: you should see 50 blue dots spread across Colorado.

2. Seasonal Sales (16 points)
An application of matrix multiplication.
When the monthly sales of a product rise and fall with the seasons, a curve that approximates the sales might have the form
\[y = a + b\,x + c\,\sin\left(2\pi\,\frac{x}{12}\right),\]
where \(x\) is the number of months since the starting point and \(y\) is the monthly sales in millions of US dollars. The term \(a + b\,x\) gives the basic trend and the sine term the seasonal change. For a brand of sunscreen whose sales are counted from June 2017 (so June 2017 is \(x = 1\)), the estimated parameters \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are supplied in the starter as model_parameters = [2, 5, 18].
Estimate the total sales for every month from June 2017 through February 2020, inclusive, with matrix multiplication. (Many sales models failed after March 2020, probably because of COVID.)

2.1 The months array (8 points)
Create a NumPy array with one row per month in the period and three columns: all 1s; the month number \(x\), from 1 to the number of months in the period; and \(\sin(2\pi x / 12)\) for each \(x\).
Hint: np.sin() applies the sine to every entry of an array at once, like the other NumPy functions in NumPy Fundamentals, and np.pi is the constant \(\pi\). Build the three columns as 1D arrays, then combine them with np.vstack() and .T from the same chapter.


2.2 The parameters array (2 points)
Create a NumPy array from model_parameters.


2.3 Monthly sales (4 points)
Use matrix multiplication to get the estimated sales for each month in the period.


2.4 Total sales (2 points)
Find the total estimated sales over the whole period.

4. Exercise Minutes (16 points)
An application of vectorized random sampling.
The list exercise_minutes, supplied in the starter, holds the weekly exercise minutes reported by students in a past STAT 303-1 class. This question finds a 95% confidence interval for the mean with bootstrapping, twice — once in plain Python and once with NumPy — and compares the time each takes.
The bootstrap method:

Let \(N\) be the number of values in exercise_minutes.
Draw \(N\) values at random, with replacement, from exercise_minutes.
Compute the mean of those \(N\) values.
Repeat steps 2 and 3 10,000 times.
The 95% confidence interval runs from the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentile of the 10,000 means.

The starter notebook supplies exercise_minutes as a Python list of 191 values.

4.1 Without NumPy (8 points)
Without NumPy, compute the confidence interval, and time the computation. This is the other question where a loop is allowed.
Hints: random.choices(exercise_minutes, k=N), from Python’s built-in random module (import random), draws \(N\) values with replacement. With the 10,000 means in a sorted list, the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles are approximately the values at positions 250 and 9,750. Time the cell with %timeit -o -r 3 -n 1, as in NumPy and pandas in a Real Workflow, and keep the result’s .average.


4.2 With NumPy (7 points)
Using NumPy and no loops, compute the same confidence interval and time it the same way.
Hint: rng = np.random.default_rng(303), then rng.choice(), which draws with replacement by default, as in NumPy Fundamentals. Passing a tuple, size=(10_000, N), returns a 2D array with one bootstrap sample per row, so .mean(axis=1) gives all 10,000 means at once. np.percentile() with [2.5, 97.5] gives both percentiles, as in the Aggregate Functions section.


4.3 Time saved (1 point)
Report the ratio of the time without NumPy to the time with NumPy.

E.1 Files and Packages
In Data Visualization II, you built figures out of panels and decided what each panel was for. This appendix answers a different question: what to do when the thing a panel should show is where. Maps answer questions about location, proximity, and geographic pattern, and they bring one requirement no other plot has — every layer has to agree about what its coordinates mean before it can be drawn on top of another.
Nothing here is required for any assignment. It is kept as a resource for final projects that involve locations, and it is written so you can read it end to end without running anything: every map below is saved with the page, including the interactive one.

This appendix has no practice kit, no activity, and no Canvas quiz. It is reference material for a project that involves locations.
This appendix ships no practice kit. Its three data files live in the coursebook’s Datasets/ folder, beside the notebook: the 2013 Divvy trip sample divvy_2013.csv, the community population layer chicago_commpop.geojson, and the community boundaries in Datasets/chicago_boundaries/. The population file is a frozen copy of the GeoDa dataset used in the original chapter; its source and retrieval details are in the data source note. Geographic data has no equivalent of seaborn’s built-in datasets, so unlike the visualization chapters there is nothing to load in one line.
Run the notebook with Datasets/ beside it, using the project environment from the setup chapters.
A shapefile is a collection: .shp stores geometry, .shx indexes it, and .dbf stores attributes; the accompanying .prj describes the CRS. Keep companion files together. GeoJSON provides geometry and attributes in one file. Both can be read with gpd.read_file().
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

import geopandas as gpd
import folium

DATA = Path("Datasets")
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", palette="colorblind", context="notebook")

text:
E.2 Read Boundaries and Inspect Their CRS
Start with the boundary layer, and look at its coordinate reference system before anything else. gpd.read_file() reads a shapefile from its .shp path and finds the companion files itself.

import geopandas as gpd
import folium

boundary_path = DATA / "chicago_boundaries" / "geo_export_26bce2f2-c163-42a9-9329-9ca6e082c5e9.shp"
chicago = gpd.read_file(boundary_path)
print("CRS:", chicago.crs)
print("Bounds:", chicago.total_bounds)
chicago[["community", "geometry"]].head()

A coordinate reference system (CRS) describes how coordinates locate places. Longitude and latitude are angular coordinates; projected coordinates may be measured in metres or feet.

set_crs(...) assigns a known interpretation to existing coordinates. It does not transform values.
to_crs(...) transforms coordinates from their known source CRS to a target CRS.

Never assign a CRS just to make mismatched layers appear compatible. Establish the source CRS from metadata first. For longitude/latitude point construction, x is longitude and y is latitude; Folium location lists use the opposite order, [latitude, longitude].

E.3 Static Boundary Map
Use neutral boundaries when the task is locating stations. A separate color and legend entry for every community area would make that task harder.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 9), layout="constrained")
chicago.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="gray", linewidth=0.5)
ax.set(title="Chicago community-area boundaries", xlabel="Longitude (degrees)", ylabel="Latitude (degrees)")
ax.grid(False)
plt.show()

title: Appendix E — Geospatial Plotting for Final Projects
section: E.4 From Trip Rows to Station Locations
text:
E.4 From Trip Rows to Station Locations
One trip row is not one station. Repeated trip origins describe use in this sample; a deduplicated station layer describes locations. We group by station ID and coordinates, retaining multiple locations if an ID moved. Missing coordinates are excluded, and counts below refer to trips with usable starting coordinates. Only observed starting stations are represented, not necessarily every station operating in 2013.
The station summary below uses .groupby(), which belongs to Data Grouping and Aggregation. If you have not met it yet, read it as “one row per station ID and coordinate pair, with the trips counted”.

trips = pd.read_csv(DATA / "divvy_2013.csv")
located_trips = trips.dropna(subset=["from_station_id", "longitude_start", "latitude_start"])
print(f"Excluded {len(trips) - len(located_trips):,} trips without a usable origin")
stations = located_trips.groupby(
    ["from_station_id", "longitude_start", "latitude_start"], as_index=False
).agg(station_name=("from_station_name", "first"), sample_trips=("trip_id", "size"))
station_points = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    stations,
    geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(stations["longitude_start"], stations["latitude_start"]),
    crs="EPSG:4326",
)
# Transform the point layer to the boundary layer's CRS before overlaying.
station_layer = station_points.to_crs(chicago.crs)
print(f"{len(station_points):,} observed station locations from {len(located_trips):,} trips")
assert int(stations["sample_trips"].sum()) == len(located_trips)

Excluded 0 trips without a usable origin
107 observed station locations from 4,005 trips



fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 9), layout="constrained")
chicago.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="gray", linewidth=0.5)
station_layer.plot(ax=ax, color="darkblue", markersize=8, alpha=0.7,
                    label="Observed starting station")
ax.set(title="Starting stations observed in the 2013 Divvy sample",
       xlabel="Longitude (degrees)", ylabel="Latitude (degrees)")
ax.legend(loc="lower left")
ax.grid(False)
plt.show()








Interpret: Where are observed origins concentrated? What can this sample tell you about station locations, and what cannot it establish about access or total ridership? Explain why plotting every trip with identical markers answers a different question and creates overplotting.

title: Appendix E — Geospatial Plotting for Final Projects
text:
E.5 Population Totals Versus Density
A choropleth shades regions by a statistic. Larger areas can contain more people simply because they cover more land. If the question concerns concentration, population density may be more useful than a total. Neither statistic answers every question.
The local population layer has 2000 and 2010 counts. Use a projected CRS with metre units to calculate square kilometres; do not calculate area directly from longitude/latitude degrees. EPSG:26916 (UTM zone 16N) is a regional projected system suitable for this Chicago teaching example. The denominator below is the area of the supplied polygon geometry; water-area treatment depends on the boundary source.

communities = gpd.read_file(DATA / "chicago_commpop.geojson")
communities_m = communities.to_crs("EPSG:26916")
communities["area_km2"] = communities_m.area / 1_000_000
communities["people_per_km2"] = communities["POP2010"] / communities["area_km2"]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 7), layout="constrained")
for ax, column, label in zip(axes, ["POP2010", "people_per_km2"],
                              ["Population (2010)", "People per km² (2010)"]):
    communities.plot(column=column, cmap="Blues", legend=True, ax=ax,
                     legend_kwds={"label": label, "shrink": 0.6},
                     edgecolor="gray", linewidth=0.2)
    ax.set_title(label)
    ax.set_axis_off()
plt.show()








Read the two legends separately: the maps have different units. Use the same color limits when comparing the same statistic across years or groups. Sequential colors suit nonnegative population values; a diverging palette is appropriate for signed change around zero.
Classification methods such as quantiles or natural breaks group values into bins. They can change the visual story. Inspect the distribution and label class boundaries if you use them; ten classes are rarely a good starting point for a small map.

section: E.6 Interactive Maps with GeoPandas and Folium
text:
E.6 Interactive Maps with GeoPandas and Folium
GeoDataFrame.explore() returns a folium.Map. It supports tooltips and popups, and a second call can add a layer using m=m. A layer selector requires folium.LayerControl(); attribute search or filtering requires extra controls or data preparation.
The vector layers are local. Interactive maps still load browser JavaScript and, with default tiles, a web basemap. Keep the static plots above as a fallback when internet access or an HTML renderer is unavailable.

m = communities.to_crs("EPSG:4326").explore(
    column="people_per_km2", cmap="Blues", legend=True,
    tooltip=["community", "POP2010", "people_per_km2"],
    tooltip_kwds={"aliases": ["Community", "Population (2010)", "People per km²"], "localize": True},
    name="Population density (2010)",
)
station_points.explore(
    m=m, color="darkred", name="Observed origins (2013 sample)",
    tooltip=["station_name", "sample_trips"],
    tooltip_kwds={"aliases": ["Starting station", "Trips in sample"]},
    marker_kwds={"radius": 3, "fill": True},
)
folium.LayerControl(collapsed=False).add_to(m)
m

Make this Notebook Trusted to load map: File -> Trust Notebook


Hover over a community or station, zoom in, and toggle the layers. Population counts refer to 2010, while the trips refer to a 2013 sample. Their overlay supplies geographic context; it does not establish a contemporaneous population-ridership relationship.
Export an interactive map to an HTML file for a project:
m.save("chicago-divvy-map.html")
Share the HTML file as well as a static figure when appropriate. Test the exported file in a browser; a screenshot cannot preserve hovering, zooming, or layer controls. Basemap attribution must remain visible.

section: E.7 Choose a Map for a Project Question
text:
E.7 Choose a Map for a Project Question

Where are locations? Plot one point per location over neutral boundaries.
How much activity occurs at locations? Aggregate events and clearly explain the size or color encoding and observation period.
How do regions compare? Choose a count, rate, or density deliberately; state its denominator and year.

A visually prominent region is not automatically the region with the greatest need, best access, or highest risk. Those claims require additional measurements and an appropriate comparison population.

title: Appendix E — Geospatial Plotting for Final Projects
text:
E.9 Before You Move On
The discipline that separates a map from a picture of a map is the coordinate reference system. Establish each layer’s CRS from its metadata, transform with to_crs() when layers must be drawn together, and never set_crs() a layer just to silence a mismatch — that declares a lie about what the numbers mean and puts your points in the wrong place without an error.
Before a map goes into a project, check that:

Every layer’s CRS is known and they agree, and any area or distance was computed in a projected CRS with metre units.
The statistic you shaded regions by is a deliberate choice among count, rate, and density, with its denominator and year stated.
Excluded rows are reported — how many locations were dropped for missing coordinates, and what that does to the claim.
The observation period of each layer is stated, and layers from different years are not implied to be contemporaneous.
An interactive map has a static fallback, and its basemap attribution is visible.

A visually prominent region is not automatically the region with the greatest need, best access, or highest risk. Those claims need additional measurements and an appropriate comparison population.
References: GeoPandas coordinate reference systems, GeoPandas interactive maps, GeoDataFrame.explore, GeoPandas mapping and plotting tools, Folium, and EPSG.io for looking up a coordinate reference system by code.
